Stone Age to Chalcolithic India
Reading India before writing
Most of India’s past has no texts. Tools, pots and bones tell the story. UPSC asks for the phases, sites and the key change from hunting to farming.
Periods and sources

Archaeology divides prehistory by tools: Palaeolithic (Old Stone Age, to about 10,000 BCE), Mesolithic (about 10,000 to 6,000 BCE), Neolithic (from about 6,000 BCE in the north-west), Chalcolithic (copper and stone, from about 3,000 BCE), then the Iron Age. Dates vary by region. Robert Bruce Foote found the first Palaeolithic tool at Pallavaram (1863).
Palaeolithic sites and ways of life

Hunting and gathering; Quartzite tools: hand-axes and cleavers (Acheulian), choppers (Soan). Sites: Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh; rock shelters, paintings), Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu; early tools), Hunsgi (Karnataka), Belan valley (UP), Soan valley (Punjab, Pakistan). People lived in caves and rock shelters and used fire. The climate was cold and dry in the late phase.
Mesolithic

Microliths (tiny stone tools) set in wood or bone; bow and arrow; fishing; first domestication of the dog; beginnings of animal herding. Sites: Bagor (Rajasthan), Adamgarh (MP; early animals), Sarai Nahar Rai and Mahadaha (UP; burials, bone tools), Langhnaj (Gujarat). Rock paintings show hunt, dance and group life.
Neolithic revolution

V. Gordon Childe coined the term: food production, pottery, polished stone axes, settled life. Mehrgarh (Baluchistan, c. 7000 BCE; wheat, barley, cattle; precursor of the Harappan culture). Burzahom (Kashmir; pit dwellings, dogs buried with masters), Chirand (Bihar; bone tools), Koldihwa (UP; earliest rice, c. 6000 BCE), Maski, Brahmagiri, Piklihal (Karnataka), Daojali Hading (Assam). Granaries, pottery, ash mounds in the south.
Chalcolithic cultures

Use of copper with stone. Villages with mud houses; painted pottery; farming of wheat, barley and millet; cattle; burial of children in house floors. Sites: Ahar-Banas (Rajasthan), Kayatha (MP), Malwa (Navdatoli), Jorwe (Maharashtra; Inamgaon, a big site with burials and a granary), Prabhas and Rangpur (Gujarat). Also Ochre Coloured Pottery and the Copper Hoards (Gangetic basin). Reasons for decline: drought and lack of metal tools.
Why this change matters

Moving to farming made villages, property and craft. Population rose. Leaders and exchange grew. It prepared the soil for the Harappan towns. The shift was slow and had many regions: in some places hunters and herders carried on beside farmers. Rock art kept the memory.
Revolution or slow change?

Childe’s “revolution” is now thought to be gradual. Scholars (Dorian Fuller, Jean-François Jarrige) debate whether Mehrgarh’s farming was local or brought from West Asia. Rice farming might have local roots. Evidence from Attirampakkam (2018 study dating tools to 385,000 years ago) has pushed the date for Middle Palaeolithic technology much earlier in India.
Why it matters today

Bhimbetka (UNESCO 2003) and many rock-art sites need protection; the ASI and state bodies manage them. Archaeological methods (carbon dating, ancient DNA) help to resolve the debates. Tribal communities still use some of these skills, and traditional crops have been revived: millets (International Year of Millets, 2023).
How to answer

“Describe the Neolithic revolution in India.” “Chalcolithic cultures: features and sites.” Prelims tip: Mehrgarh (earliest farming), Burzahom (pit dwellings), Koldihwa (rice), Jorwe (Inamgaon), Bagor (Mesolithic, animals), Bhimbetka (UNESCO).
The Harappan Civilisation
India’s first cities
The Indus or Harappan civilisation is the oldest urban culture of the subcontinent. It is asked every year: sites, planning, trade, decline and the script.
Discovery and extent

Dayaram Sahni found Harappa (1921); R. D. Banerji, Mohenjo-daro (1922); John Marshall was director general of the ASI. Mature phase: 2600 to 1900 BCE. Spread: Punjab, Sindh, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana, western UP, Afghanistan (Shortugai). Sites: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira , Lothal , Kalibangan , Banawali , Rakhigarhi (largest in India), Chanhudaro , Surkotada, Ropar. Named “Indus Valley”, but many sites lay on the Ghaggar-Hakra.
Town planning

Grid pattern; streets crossing at right angles; two parts: citadel (west) and lower town (east); baked brick in the ratio 1:2:4; covered drains with soak pits; the Great Bath (Mohenjo-daro); granaries (Harappa, Mohenjo-daro); Dholavira’s three parts and water reservoirs (UNESCO 2021); Lothal’s dockyard. Houses with courtyards, bathrooms and wells.
Economy and trade

Wheat, barley, cotton, dates, peas; cattle (humped bull), sheep, goat. No clear evidence of the plough in most sites (a furrowed field at Kalibangan). Crafts: beads (Chanhudaro), pottery, bronze and copper work, seals of steatite. Trade : Mesopotamia (Meluhha in Sumerian texts); Persian Gulf, Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan; weights in multiples of 16; a lack of coins (barter). Raw materials: lapis lazuli (Shortugai), copper (Khetri), tin, shell.
Society, religion, art

Seals show the Pashupati figure, unicorn bull, and trees. Mother goddess terracotta; Lingam and yoni stones; tree and animal worship; fire altars at Kalibangan and Lothal. Bronze Dancing Girl , steatite Priest-King. Burial: extended burials, pot burials. Society: no clear palaces or temples, suggesting a different form of authority.
The script

About 400 signs on seals, mostly short; written right to left (boustrophedon in some). Not yet deciphered despite many attempts (Asko Parpola: Dravidian; S. R. Rao and others: Sanskrit-like; Iravatham Mahadevan: Dravidian). Without a bilingual text, decipherment is stalled. The Dholavira signboard of ten large signs is a famous find.
Decline

Theories: shift of the Saraswati-Ghaggar river and drought (4.2 ka event); flooding (Mohenjo-daro); Aryan invasion (Wheeler, now widely rejected); trade collapse; ecological stress. The mature phase ended about 1900 BCE; urban features faded, with late Harappan villages in the east. Most scholars favour gradual climate-linked decline and migration over invasion.
Aryans and Harappans

Wheeler (1947) read Rig Veda’s purandara as conquest of Harappan cities. Later, no evidence of mass violence was found at Mohenjo-daro. Ancient DNA work points two ways: the Rakhigarhi genome (Shinde et al., 2019) has no steppe ancestry, while Narasimhan et al. (2019) show steppe pastoralist ancestry entering South Asia around 2000 to 1500 BCE. The debate on origins is both scientific and political. Make a balanced answer.
Why it matters today

Dholavira (Gujarat) became a World Heritage Site in 2021; Lothal’s National Maritime Heritage Complex is under construction. Rakhigarhi is being developed as a museum. The Harappan drains and water management are cited in modern town planning; Kutch and Rajasthan water storage echo it. Pakistan holds Harappa and Mohenjo-daro (UNESCO since 1980).
How to answer

“Describe the town planning of the Harappan civilisation.” “Why did the Harappan civilisation decline?” “Harappan trade with other regions.” Prelims tip: Lothal (dockyard), Kalibangan (fire altars, furrows), Dholavira (water, signboard), Rakhigarhi (largest in India), Mohenjo-daro (Great Bath), Chanhudaro (beads).
Harappan Sites and Their Features
Sites are Prelims gold

Almost every Prelims paper that touches the Indus civilisation asks which site has what . Learn the sites as a map: what was found, who excavated, which river, which modern state. Over 1,000 sites are known, but about a dozen carry the questions.
The big five cities

Harappa (Punjab, Pakistan, on the Ravi): found by Daya Ram Sahni (1921); granaries, cemetery H, a stone dancing figure. Mohenjodaro (Sindh, on the Indus): R. D. Banerji (1922); the Great Bath, the Granary, the Pashupati seal, the bronze dancing girl. Dholavira (Kutch, Gujarat): J. P. Joshi and later R. S. Bisht; Rakhigarhi (Haryana): the largest Indian site; Ganweriwala (Cholistan): unexcavated.
Dholavira, the water city

Dholavira lies on Khadir island in the Rann of Kutch. It has three divisions (citadel, middle town, lower town) instead of two, huge stepped reservoirs and channels for rain water, and a signboard with ten large letters of the script. UNESCO inscribed it in 2021 , India’s first Harappan World Heritage site, as “Dholavira: A Harappan City”.
Port and craft towns

Lothal (Gujarat, near Bhogavo): S. R. Rao; a brick dock, bead factory, rice husk, a terracotta ship model, fire altars. Chanhudaro (Sindh): bead-making, no citadel; Mackay. Balakot : shell work. Kalibangan (Rajasthan, Ghaggar): ploughed field, fire altars, camel bones, bangles; B. B. Lal and B. K. Thapar. Banawali (Haryana): barley, a radial street plan.
Site and signature find
North, west and east limits

Manda (Jammu, on the Chenab) is the northern limit; Alamgirpur (Meerut, UP, on the Hindon) the eastern; Daimabad (Maharashtra, on the Pravara) the southern; Sutkagen Dor (Makran coast, Pakistan) the western. Daimabad has the famous bronze chariot and rhino, though some scholars link it to late Harappan or Jorwe culture.
Other sites worth knowing

Surkotada (Kutch): the first actual horse bones, found by J. P. Joshi. Rangpur (Gujarat): rice husk, a Late Harappan site. Ropar (Punjab, Sutlej): the first Harappan site excavated after Independence, a dog buried with a human. Sokhta Koh and Shortughai (Afghanistan): trading posts for lapis lazuli. Sanauli (Baghpat, UP): burials with chariot remains, later than Harappan.
Open questions

Rakhigarhi’s 2018 to 2019 DNA study of a female skeleton found no steppe ancestry, which supporters use to argue continuity. Many scholars link the dry Ghaggar-Hakra bed to the Vedic Sarasvati; others dispute this. Treat all of it as debated. Mohenjodaro also shows no clear palace, so who ruled remains unknown.
Why it matters today

The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) protects sites under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958. Dholavira (2021) shows heritage tourism and water-harvesting lessons. A proposed National Maritime Heritage Complex at Lothal is under development.
How to answer

“Match site and discovery” (Lothal: dock; Kalibangan: ploughed field; Surkotada: horse). “Which was the first Harappan site excavated after 1947?” (Ropar). Mains: “Harappan town planning shows a high degree of civic sense. Discuss.” Use grid, drains, three-part Dholavira, dock at Lothal. Always attach river and state.
Sources of Ancient History: Inscriptions and Coins
Evidence beats legend

Ancient India has few year-by-year chronicles. Historians rebuild the past from inscriptions, coins, monuments, foreign accounts and literature . Prelims loves matching an inscription to its ruler and language.
Epigraphy and numismatics

Epigraphy studies inscriptions; numismatics studies coins; palaeography studies old scripts. Inscriptions on rock, pillar, copper plate and temple wall record grants, victories and orders. Coins date events, show trade and rulers’ religion.
Deciphering Brahmi

James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi and Kharosthi in 1837, helped by bilingual Greek-Indian coins, and read “Devanampiya Piyadasi” on Ashokan edicts. Only in 1915 did the Maski edict (Karnataka) name Ashoka directly. Brahmi runs left to right; Kharosthi right to left, used in the north-west.
Famous inscriptions

Hathigumpha (Kharavela of Kalinga, Odisha, Jaina king); Junagadh rock inscription (Rudradaman, c. 150 CE, first long Sanskrit inscription, Sudarshana lake); Allahabad Pillar (Samudragupta, by Harisena); Aihole (Pulakeshin II, by Ravikirti, 634 CE); Mehrauli iron pillar (Chandra); Uttaramerur (Parantaka Chola, village assembly rules); Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar (Vaishnavism).
Types of source
Coins tell stories

Punch-marked coins (karshapana) are the oldest, silver, c. 6th century BCE. Indo-Greek kings first put names and portraits on coins. Kushanas issued gold; Guptas issued fine gold dinaras (Samudragupta playing the veena). Satavahana lead coins show ships. Hoards show trade with Rome.
Foreign and literary accounts

Megasthenes (Indica, in Chandragupta’s court), Fa-Hien (Gupta India), Hsuan Tsang (Harsha), Al-Biruni (Kitab-ul-Hind, 11th century), Kalhana’s Rajatarangini (12th century), the only real historical text from ancient India. Sangam poems and Kautilya’s Arthashastra complete the picture.
Bias and gaps

Royal inscriptions praise kings; they may exaggerate victory. Many texts were later edited. Archaeologists cross-check, for example the Greek claim of Chandragupta meeting Seleucus with the Mauryan record. No source gives a full picture alone.
Today’s link

The ASI’s Epigraphy branch is at Mysuru; “Epigraphia Indica” publishes finds. The Indian Treasure Trove Act, 1878 requires reporting coin hoards. The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972 regulates sale of antiquities. Classical language status for Tamil and others depends on old inscriptions and texts.
How to answer

“Which ruler is linked to Hathigumpha / Junagadh / Aihole inscription?” “Why are inscriptions more reliable than literature?” Prelims tip: Prinsep (1837), Rajatarangini (Kashmir), Kharosthi right to left. Mains: Evaluate sources for Mauryan or Gupta history in 150 words.
Vedic Society, Polity and Economy
From pastoral tribes to kingdoms
The Vedic age sits between the Harappans and the Mahajanapadas. You need to tell Early and Later Vedic apart. Questions mix texts, society, polity and the economy.
Sources and dating

The Rig Veda (earliest, c. 1500 to 1000 BCE) and later Vedas (Sama, Yajur, Atharva), Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads (c. 1000 to 600 BCE). Archaeology: Painted Grey Ware (PGW) culture in the Ganga-Yamuna doab links to Later Vedic. The Aryans’ origin is a debate (see below). Vedanga and Sutra texts followed.
Early Vedic (Rig Vedic) period

Saptasindhu region. Society: tribal ( jana ); family ( kula ); the rajan was a tribal chief, assisted by the purohita (Vashishtha, Vishvamitra) and senani . Assemblies: Sabha, Samiti, Vidatha, Gana . Economy: cattle ( gau , gavishthi for war), pastoralism, limited agriculture; nishka as ornament, barter. Gods: Indra (war), Agni, Varuna, Soma. Women: Ghosha, Lopamudra, Apala; the Dasarajna battle (ten kings) on the Parushni (Ravi). Varna mentioned only in the Purusha Sukta , a late hymn.
Later Vedic period

Shift east to the Ganga-Yamuna doab and Kosala-Kashi (c. 1000 to 600 BCE). Larger kingdoms ( janapadas ): Kuru, Panchala. Rulers performed Rajasuya , Ashvamedha , Vajapeya . The Sabha and Samiti declined; the kingdom grew with bali (tax) and sangrihitri (treasurer). Society: four varnas firmly formed; ashrama system ( Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha, Sanyasa ); gotra . Women lost status somewhat.
Later Vedic economy

Agriculture became main: iron ( shyama ayas , krishna ayas ; iron from about 1000 to 800 BCE at sites such as Atranjikhera), plough, rice ( vrihi ), wheat, barley; sali . Crafts: carpenters, smiths, potters, weavers; trade; nishka and satamana as proto-currency; PGW and NBPW pottery. Cities emerged only later, around 600 BCE.
Religion and philosophy

Early: nature gods and sacrifices ( yajna ), no temples. Later: ritual complexity, priestly power ( Brahmanas ); Prajapati, Vishnu and Rudra rose; Indra declined. Upanishads: Brahman and Atman , karma , moksha ; “Satyameva Jayate” from the Mundaka Upanishad. Ritual debates gave rise to Buddhism and Jainism.
Epics and Smritis

The Ramayana and the Mahabharata took their form between about 400 BCE and 400 CE. Dharmasutras (Gautama, Apastamba) and later Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE to 200 CE) set social and legal norms. These are used with caution, as they are composite texts.
Who were the Aryans?

Max Müller (1850s) proposed Aryan migration from Central Asia. Indian writers (B. G. Tilak: Arctic home; others: Indian origin) argued differently. Linguists point to Indo-European roots. Genetics (Narasimhan et al. 2019) shows steppe ancestry in many South Asians after 2000 BCE, while the Harappan genome from Rakhigarhi (Shinde et al. 2019) has none. Historians such as Romila Thapar stress that “Aryan” is a linguistic term, not a race. The debate remains charged.
Why it matters today

The Mundaka line “Satyameva Jayate” is India’s national motto. Sabha and Samiti are cited in discussions of Indian democratic roots; the Lok Sabha and Parliament use these words. The ashrama and varna ideas remain in social debates. Yajna and Vedic chanting are on UNESCO’s ICH list (Vedic chanting, 2008).
How to answer

“Differentiate between Early and Later Vedic society and polity.” “Why did the Sabha and Samiti decline?” Prelims tip: Sabha, Samiti, Vidatha; Purusha Sukta; Dasarajna; PGW = Later Vedic; Sangrihitri; iron around 1000 BCE; Satyameva Jayate = Mundaka Upanishad.
Buddhism, Jainism and the Mahajanapadas
A new age of thought and states
About 600 BCE the Ganga plains saw the second urbanisation, new kingdoms and religions that questioned ritual. This sets the stage for the Mauryas.
Why new religions arose

Rituals and sacrifices were costly; Brahmin dominance and the varna order irked Kshatriyas and Vaishyas. Iron ploughs and trade made merchants rich; they wanted respect. Cities and coins grew. Reformers offered simple, ethical paths in local languages.
Buddhism

Siddhartha Gautama (c. 563 to 483 BCE, Lumbini); enlightenment at Bodh Gaya; first sermon at Sarnath ( Dharmachakra Pravartana ); died at Kushinagar. Four Noble Truths : suffering, its cause (craving), its end ( nirvana ), the Eightfold Path . Middle Path , anatta , karma . The Sangha admitted women (Mahaprajapati Gotami). Councils: Rajagriha (483 BCE), Vaishali (383 BCE), Pataliputra (Ashoka, c. 250 BCE), Kashmir (Kanishka). Sects: Theravada, Mahayana (Nagarjuna), Vajrayana. Texts: Tripitaka in Pali.
Jainism

Vardhamana Mahavira , the 24th Tirthankara (c. 540 to 468 BCE, Vaishali). Predecessor Parshvanatha. Five vows ( ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha, brahmacharya ); three jewels (right faith, knowledge, conduct); anekantavada (many-sidedness of truth). Split into Digambara (Bhadrabahu) and Svetambara (Sthulabhadra) after famine around 300 BCE; the council at Pataliputra and Vallabhi (512 CE). Patrons: Bimbisara, Ajatashatru, Chandragupta Maurya, Kharavela of Kalinga, Chalukyas.
The 16 Mahajanapadas

Anguttara Nikaya lists 16 (Kashi, Kosala, Anga, Magadha, Vajji, Malla, Chedi, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchala, Machchha, Surasena, Assaka, Avanti, Gandhara, Kamboja). Most were monarchies; some were gana-sanghas (republics) such as the Vajji (Vaishali) and Malla. Capitals: Rajagriha, Shravasti, Ujjain, Kaushambi. Coins: punch-marked silver karshapana . Fortified cities.
Rise of Magadha

Reasons: fertile plains, nearby iron mines, rivers for trade, elephants, strong rulers. Haryanka : Bimbisara (c. 544 to 492 BCE; Anga annexed; marriages), Ajatashatru (Vajji war; first Council), Udayin (Pataliputra). Shishunaga dynasty. Nanda dynasty: Mahapadma Nanda, “sole sovereign” (c. 345 BCE), large army; their wealth. Alexander invaded in 326 BCE (battle of the Hydaspes against Porus) and his army refused to go further.
Society and economy

Second urbanisation: Rajagriha, Vaishali, Kaushambi, Ujjain. Guilds ( shrenis ), the setthi (merchant), trade routes ( Uttarapatha ). Gahapati landholders. Social mobility for merchants. Iron tools, NBPW pottery (Northern Black Polished Ware), coins. Women of the Sangha and Jaina nuns show new paths.
Why did Buddhism decline in India?

Reasons offered: revival of Brahmanism (Shankara, bhakti), Buddhist splits and monastic wealth, loss of royal patronage, invasions (Huns, Turks) and destruction of monasteries (Nalanda, c. 1200). Scholars such as D. N. Jha and Romila Thapar caution against single causes; Buddhism spread widely abroad. B. R. Ambedkar wrote on Buddha and his Dhamma (1957) and on the reasons for decline.
Why it matters today

The Ashoka Chakra on the flag and the lion capital are Buddhist symbols. Ambedkar’s conversion (14 October 1956, Nagpur) shaped Dalit politics. Buddhist circuit tourism (Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar; Kushinagar airport 2021), the Nalanda University revival (2010 Act, new campus in 2024), and the Jain concept of aparigraha in sustainability debates link the past to now.
How to answer

“Why did Magadha become the most powerful Mahajanapada?” “Compare Buddhism and Jainism.” “Causes of the rise of new religions in the 6th century BCE.” Prelims tip: Sarnath first sermon; Kushinagar mahaparinirvana; Mahavira = 24th; Digambara and Svetambara; Hydaspes 326 BCE; Haryanka–Shishunaga–Nanda order.
Buddhist Councils and Sects
How the Buddha’s word was fixed
The Buddha taught orally. Councils (sangitis) were held to settle the teachings and rules. Prelims asks place, patron and president of each council. Their disputes also explain the rise of Mahayana.
The Tripitaka

The Pali canon has three baskets: Vinaya Pitaka (monastic rules), Sutta Pitaka (discourses), Abhidhamma Pitaka (philosophy). Vinaya was recited by Upali , Sutta by Ananda . Abhidhamma is traditionally traced to the Third Council.
First and Second Councils

First (c. 483 BCE): Rajgriha, Sattapanni cave, patron Ajatashatru (Haryanka), president Mahakassapa , soon after the Buddha’s death. Second (c. 383 BCE): Vaishali, patron Kalashoka (Shishunaga), president Sabakami ; split over ten points of discipline, such as accepting money. Two groups emerged: Sthaviravadins (elders) and Mahasanghikas.
Third Council

Third (c. 250 BCE): Pataliputra, patron Ashoka , president Moggaliputta Tissa . It expelled heretics, settled the Abhidhamma, and the Kathavatthu was composed. Ashoka then sent missions to Sri Lanka (Mahinda and Sanghamitta), Gandhara and elsewhere. This council was held by Theravadins and is not accepted by all schools.
Fourth Council

Fourth (c. 72 CE or 1st century CE): Kundalvana, Kashmir (some say Jalandhar), patron Kanishka , president Vasumitra with Ashvaghosha as vice-president. Sanskrit was adopted; the Mahavibhasha commentary was compiled. It confirmed the split into Hinayana (Theravada) and Mahayana .
Four councils
Sects and schools

Theravada : Sri Lanka and South-East Asia, Pali, arhat ideal. Mahayana : bodhisattva ideal, Buddha as god, image worship, Sanskrit; Nagarjuna (Madhyamika) and Asanga, Vasubandhu (Yogachara). Vajrayana : tantra, rituals, Tibet and Bhutan; Padmasambhava. Sarvastivadins and Sautrantikas are Hinayana schools.
Historical or traditional?

Scholars doubt the exact dates and even whether the First Council was a formal event. The Second is better supported. Ashoka’s own edicts do not mention the Third. Dates of Kanishka (78 CE Saka era or later) are also debated.
Living legacy

Nalanda University was revived in Bihar (2010 Act; new campus 2024) and its ruins are a World Heritage Site (2016). Buddhist circuit tourism connects Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar. Dhamma Chakra Day (Ashokan conversions) and Buddha Purnima are observed.
How to answer

“Match council, patron and place.” “Why did Buddhism split into Hinayana and Mahayana?” Mains: Role of Ashoka and Kanishka in spreading Buddhism. Prelims: Third council president Moggaliputta Tissa; Kathavatthu.
Jain Councils and Sects
Small religion, steady questions
Jainism gets fewer pages than Buddhism but the same Prelims attention: tirthankaras, councils, Digambara and Svetambara, the five vows and Jain art. The 2-3 question pattern is stable.
24 Tirthankaras

The first was Rishabhanatha (Adinatha), symbol bull. Parshvanatha (23rd, symbol snake) was born at Varanasi, c. 8th century BCE, and taught four vows. Mahavira (24th, symbol lion) was born c. 540 BCE at Kundagrama near Vaishali, a Jnatrika kshatriya; he left home at 30, gained kevala jnana at 42 under a sal tree on the Rijupalika bank, died at Pavapuri (Rajgir) c. 468 BCE.
Teachings

Five mahavratas : ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha and brahmacharya. Mahavira added the fifth to Parshva’s four. Triratna : right faith, right knowledge, right conduct. Anekantavada (many-sidedness), syadvada , no creator god, karma as fine matter. Language: Ardhamagadhi Prakrit.
First Council, Pataliputra

Held c. 300 BCE under Sthulabhadra after a 12-year famine; Bhadrabahu had gone south with Chandragupta Maurya (tradition) to Shravanabelagola, Karnataka. The 12 Angas (a 12th, Drishtivada, was lost) were compiled by the monks who stayed. The southern group rejected them. Tradition makes this the cause of the split.
Second Council, Valabhi

Held at Valabhi (Gujarat) c. 512 CE (454 CE by some) under Devardhi Kshamashramana . The Jain canon was written down: 12 Angas, 12 Upangas, 10 Prakirnakas, 6 Chedasutras, 4 Mulasutras. Digambaras do not accept these texts as authentic.
The two sects
Sects compared

Svetambaras : white robes, women can attain liberation, Mahavira married (some say). Digambaras : monks naked, women cannot gain moksha without rebirth, Mahavira unmarried. Sub-sects: Murtipujaka, Sthanakvasi, Terapanthi; Digambara Bispanthi and Terapanthi. Patrons: Chandragupta Maurya, Kharavela, Rashtrakutas, Gangas, Solanki rulers.
Jain art

Shravanabelagola’s Gommateshvara (Bahubali) statue, c. 981 CE, Chamundaraya (Ganga minister). Dilwara temples , Mount Abu (marble, Solanki, 11th to 13th century). Ranakpur, Palitana, Khandagiri-Udayagiri caves. Kalpasutra manuscripts and miniatures are early paper and palm-leaf painting.
Today

Jains are about 0.4 per cent of India’s population (Census 2011). They were recognised as a national minority in 2014 under the NCM Act. Paryushana, Mahamastakabhisheka (every 12 years at Shravanabelagola; last in 2018) are major events. Ahimsa influenced Gandhi.
How to answer
“Distinguish Jainism from Buddhism.” “Why did Jainism remain in India while Buddhism spread abroad?” Prelims: symbols of tirthankaras, Parshva’s 4 vs Mahavira’s 5 vows, Valabhi.
The Mauryan Empire
India’s first big empire
The Mauryas (c. 321 to 185 BCE) united most of the subcontinent. We have rich sources: Kautilya, Megasthenes, Ashoka’s edicts. Ashoka’s Dhamma is a regular Mains theme.
Sources

Arthashastra (Kautilya or Chanakya; dating disputed, between c. 300 BCE and 300 CE, with the core from Mauryan times). Indica (Megasthenes, Greek ambassador at Chandragupta’s court; survives in fragments). Mudrarakshasa (Vishakhadatta, Gupta period). Buddhist texts ( Dipavamsa , Mahavamsa ), Jain texts, Ashokan inscriptions, Rudradaman’s Junagadh inscription (Sudarshana lake).
Chandragupta and Bindusara

Chandragupta Maurya (c. 321 to 297 BCE), with Chanakya, overthrew the Nandas, defeated Seleucus Nicator (c. 305 BCE; treaty gave Kabul, Kandahar, Herat and Baluchistan for 500 elephants; Megasthenes sent). Later, tradition says he became a Jain monk (Shravanabelagola). Bindusara (c. 297 to 273 BCE): “Amitraghata” (slayer of foes); extended to the Deccan; ties with Syria (Antiochus I) and Egypt.
Ashoka and Kalinga

Ashoka (c. 268 to 232 BCE). Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE; Rock Edict XIII: 100,000 killed, 150,000 deported): he turned to Buddhism and Dhamma . Edicts in Brahmi (and Kharosthi, Greek, Aramaic in the west) on rocks and pillars; discovered by James Prinsep (1837 deciphered Brahmi). Rock Edicts, Minor Rock Edicts, Pillar Edicts (Delhi-Topra, Sarnath), Lauriya Nandangarh. He is called “Devanampiya Piyadasi”.
Ashoka’s Dhamma

Not a new religion but a moral code: tolerance, non-violence to animals, respect to elders, kindness to slaves, truth, generosity. Dhamma-mahamattas (appointed in the 13th year) took the message; tours ( dhamma-yatras ), welfare (wells, trees, hospitals, rest houses), peace with neighbours, envoys to Sri Lanka (Mahinda and Sanghamitra), Syria, Egypt, Macedonia. Ashokan lion capital at Sarnath is India’s emblem; the wheel is on the flag. Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra.
Mauryan administration

Highly centralised. Saptanga (seven limbs of the state). King; mantri-parishad ; Amatyas ; 18 tirthas (officials) in the Arthashastra. Provinces: Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali, Suvarnagiri, Pataliputra ( Kumaras as governors). Local: Gopa , Sthanika ; Pradeshika , Rajuka , Yukta . Megasthenes: six committees of five members each in Pataliputra. A vast spy network ( gudhapurushas ). A standing army (600,000 infantry per Pliny). Revenue: bhaga (one-sixth), bali , sita (crown lands), taxes on trade; state control of mines and the economy.
Economy and society

Agriculture, state farms ( sita ), irrigation (Sudarshana lake), trade by Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha, punch-marked coins, guilds. Material: NBPW. Slaves ( dasa ), foreigners ( Yavanas ). Pataliputra was among the largest cities. Decline: weak successors, an expensive army and bureaucracy, tax pressure, Ashoka’s policies, provincial revolts, the rise of regions; Pushyamitra Shunga killed Brihadratha, the last Maurya (c. 185 BCE).
Ashoka: saint or statesman?

Romila Thapar ( Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas , 1961) shows Dhamma as a policy of social cohesion in a diverse empire. D. D. Kosambi and R. S. Sharma see Mauryan state as exploitative. Ashoka’s non-violence is also debated: he did not disband the army or end the death penalty. The Arthashastra’s realism (Kautilya) vs Ashoka’s idealism is a classic comparison.
Why it matters today

The Ashoka Chakra is on the flag and the Lion Capital is the State Emblem; “Satyameva Jayate” is added beneath. Ideas of welfare state, ethical governance and tolerance (Article 25) are often linked to Dhamma. The Arthashastra shapes India’s strategic thought; Pataliputra’s remains lie under Patna. Ashokan edicts are Brahmi examples in UNESCO’s tentative list.
How to answer

“Ashoka’s Dhamma: was it a religion or a policy?” “Mauryan administration: its main features.” “Why did the Mauryan Empire decline?” Prelims tip: Rock Edict XIII = Kalinga; Brahmi deciphered by Prinsep (1837); Megasthenes = Indica; Sarnath capital; Saptanga; Junagadh = Rudradaman.
Post-Mauryan Kingdoms and the Sangam Age
Foreign contact and southern flowering
After 185 BCE there was no single empire for 500 years. Instead Shungas, Satavahanas, Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas and the Sangam kingdoms shaped trade, art and language.
North India

Shungas (Pushyamitra, c. 185 BCE): Bharhut stupa, Patanjali’s Mahabhashya; Kanvas . Indo-Greeks (Demetrius, Menander or Milinda; the first to issue gold coins, with legends; Milinda-panha with Nagasena). Shakas (Rudradaman, Junagadh inscription, c. 150 CE; first major Sanskrit inscription). Parthians (Gondophernes; St Thomas tradition).
Kushanas

Kujula Kadphises founded the empire; Kanishka (c. 78 CE; the Shaka era began, traditionally dated to 78 CE) had capitals at Peshawar (Purushapura) and Mathura. Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir; patrons of Ashvaghosha, Charaka, Nagarjuna. Gold coins; Gandhara and Mathura art; Silk Route trade. Mahayana Buddhism grew. Decline in the 3rd century.
Satavahanas

Deccan power (c. 1st century BCE to 3rd century CE; capital Pratishthana (Paithan); Simuka founded). Gautamiputra Satakarni (defeated the Shakas; Nasik inscription by his mother Gautami Balashri) and Vasishthiputra Pulumavi . Features: matronymics; Prakrit; land grants to Brahmins and monks; lead coins; ports (Broach, Sopara); Buddhist art (Karle, Nasik, Amaravati). Gathasaptashati (Hala).
The Sangam age

The Tamil Sangam literature (c. 300 BCE to 300 CE) came from assemblies at Madurai. The three kingdoms: Cholas (Uraiyur, Puhar; Karikala, who built the Kallanai dam on the Kaveri), Cheras (Vanji; Senguttuvan), Pandyas (Madurai; port of Korkai). Chiefs ( velir ), eight lands ( tinai ). Texts: Tolkappiyam (grammar), Ettuthokai , Pattuppattu , the twin epics Silappadikaram and Manimekalai , and the Tirukkural .
Trade with Rome

The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (c. 1st century CE) and Pliny’s Natural History describe Indian ports. Pepper, pearls, ivory, muslin and gems went west; gold and wine came. Roman coins found in Arikamedu (Pondicherry; Wheeler excavated), Muziris (Kerala; Pattanam), Kodumanal. Monsoon winds (Hippalus, c. 50 CE tradition). Trade guilds. Satavahana and Sangam ports flourished; decline when Rome weakened (3rd century).
Society and religion

Brahmanism, Buddhism, Jainism; rise of Bhagavatism (Besnagar pillar of Heliodorus, 2nd century BCE) and devotion to Vishnu and Shiva. Foreigners were absorbed as vratya Kshatriyas. Varna ideas in the Manusmriti. Sangam society: no strict varna; mother-goddess and Murugan; tinai by region; women poets (Avvaiyar). Sati and widowhood are mentioned in Sangam poems.
Sangam dating and state

Dating of the Sangam texts runs from 300 BCE to 300 CE, with some scholars placing them later. K. A. Nilakanta Sastri accepted the traditional view; later historians (Kesavan Veluthat, Y. Subbarayalu) see a lineage-based chiefly society moving towards state formation. Another debate: were the Kushanas and Satavahanas “feudal”? R. S. Sharma argues the land grants prepared the ground for feudalism.
Why it matters today

Tamil was given classical status in 2004; the Sangam texts anchor its claim. Keezhadi (Tamil Nadu) excavations show an urban Sangam-age culture; its dating is debated: some samples are dated to about the 6th century BCE, others to the 3rd, and the ASI has asked for the earliest dates to be re-justified. Muziris Heritage Project (Kerala) and Roman coin finds feed India’s maritime heritage. The Kushana art of Gandhara links India with Afghanistan.
How to answer

“Sangam society and economy.” “Indo-Roman trade: evidence and impact.” “Contribution of the Kushanas to Indian culture.” Prelims tip: Gondophernes; Kanishka (78 CE Shaka era); Gautamiputra Satakarni; Karikala; Arikamedu; Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal); Tolkappiyam; classical Tamil 2004.
The Gupta Age
The “classical age”
The Guptas (c. 320 to 550 CE) are remembered for art, science and Sanskrit. Historians debate whether it was a golden age. Questions test rulers, sources and cultural achievements.
Rise of the Guptas

Founder: Sri Gupta ; Chandragupta I (c. 319 to 335 CE) married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi (Gupta era from 319 or 320 CE). Capital Pataliputra, later Ayodhya and Ujjain. Sources: coins, the Allahabad Pillar (Prayaga Prashasti), Fa-Hien’s travel account, Kalidasa, Vishakhadatta’s Devichandraguptam , Mehrauli iron pillar.
Samudragupta (c. 335 to 375)

Called the “Napoleon of India” (V. A. Smith). The Prayaga Prashasti by Harishena records his conquests: Aryavarta (violent conquest), Dakshinapatha (captured and then freed: grahana-moksha-anugraha ), forest tribes, frontier kings; foreign kings offered gifts. Performed Ashvamedha. Coins show him playing the veena. Patron of Vasubandhu; Sri Lankan king Meghavarna sent a mission.
Chandragupta II and later rulers

Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) , c. 375 to 415 CE: defeated the Shakas of Western India (Rudrasimha III), gaining ports (Bharuch) and Ujjain; Navaratnas (Kalidasa, Amarasimha, Varahamihira); Fa-Hien visited. Kumaragupta I (c. 415 to 455): Nalanda founded. Skandagupta : repelled the Hunas; Sudarshana lake repaired. Later Guptas fell to the Huns (Toramana, Mihirakula) and regional rulers by about 550 CE.
Administration

Titles: Maharajadhiraja , Parameshvara . Provinces ( bhuktis , under uparikas ), districts ( vishayas , under vishayapatis ), villages ( gramikas ). Officers: Mahasandhivigrahika , Kumaramatya , Dandanayaka . A more decentralised pattern than the Mauryas: feudatories ( samantas ), land grants ( agrahara ), religious grants with administrative rights. Brahmin and temple lands grew. Fewer salaried officials, more land payment.
Economy

Fa-Hien noted safe roads and mild taxes. Gold coins ( dinaras ) in large numbers, but fewer silver and copper coins and a decline in long-distance trade in the later period (R. S. Sharma). Crafts: textiles, ivory, metallurgy (the Delhi Iron Pillar of Chandragupta II). Land grants and forced labour ( vishti ) increased. Towns declined according to some historians.
Culture and science

Literature : Kalidasa ( Shakuntala , Meghaduta , Raghuvamsha ), Shudraka, Vishakhadatta, Bharavi; Panchatantra ; Puranas and Smritis (Narada, Brihaspati) compiled; Science : Aryabhata ( Aryabhatiya , 499 CE; zero, decimal, the earth’s rotation, pi), Varahamihira ( Brihat Samhita ), Brahmagupta (later), Sushruta and Charaka (earlier works). Art : Deogarh Dashavatara temple, Sarnath Buddha, Ajanta, Udayagiri. Nalanda grew into a great university.
Golden age or not?

Nationalist historians (R. C. Majumdar, Altekar) called it a golden age. Marxist historians (R. S. Sharma, D. N. Jha) said it was the start of feudalism with landlordism, decline of trade and rise of untouchability (Fa-Hien’s mention of chandalas ). Romila Thapar urges care with the term. Recent work stresses regional variety. The age had great art, science and literature but also growing social rigidity and worsening position of women (child marriage, restrictions in Smritis).
Why it matters today

The Delhi Iron Pillar shows India’s early metallurgy; Aryabhata gave his name to India’s first satellite (1975). “Nalanda” inspired the new Nalanda University. Aryabhata’s zero and the decimal system are India’s contribution to global mathematics. Yet the golden age claim features in culture and history textbook debates.
How to answer

“Was the Gupta age a golden age?” “Gupta administration compared with the Mauryan.” “Contribution of the Guptas to science and art.” Prelims tip: Prayaga Prashasti = Harishena; Fa-Hien = Chandragupta II; Aryabhatiya 499; Navaratnas; Mehrauli pillar; Nalanda = Kumaragupta I; Huns = Skandagupta.
Mauryan Art and Architecture
First imperial art
Mauryan art is the first large body of stone art in India. Prelims asks about pillars, stupas, caves, polish and the Didarganj Yakshi . It also shows two streams: court art and popular art.
Court art and popular art

Court art : Ashokan pillars, palace at Kumrahar (Pataliputra, with an 80-pillar hall, Persepolis-like). Popular art : Yaksha and Yakshi figures, terracotta, caves. Wood was used earlier; Ashoka moved to stone. Foreign influence (Persian, Greek) is debated.
Ashokan pillars

Monolithic, of Chunar sandstone, 12 to 15 m tall, with a smooth Mauryan polish and an animal capital on a bell-shaped lotus base and abacus. Examples: Lauriya Nandangarh, Sanchi, Rampurva (bull, lion), Sankisa (elephant), Allahabad (Kosambi), Sarnath. The Sarnath lion capital has four lions and four wheels on the abacus; India’s state emblem, adopted 26 January 1950, comes from it.
Stupas

Ashoka is credited with 84,000 stupas. Sanchi’s Great Stupa (Madhya Pradesh) began under Ashoka as a brick stupa; the stone casing and toranas came later (Shunga, Satavahana). Bharhut and Sanchi stupas show Buddha as symbols: wheel, footprints, bodhi tree. A stupa has anda, harmika, chhatra, medhi and vedika.
Parts of a pillar
Rock-cut caves

The Barabar and Nagarjuni hills (Bihar) caves were donated to Ajivikas by Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha. Lomas Rishi cave has a carved elephant frieze. The walls have a mirror polish. Caves imitate wooden huts. They begin the tradition of rock-cut architecture later seen at Karle and Ajanta.
Sculpture

The Didarganj Yakshi (Patna museum) stands about 1.6 m, polished sandstone, a Mauryan masterpiece. Parkham Yaksha (Mathura), Besnagar Yakshi, Dhauli elephant (Odisha, the first Buddhist rock sculpture). The Rampurva bull shows Persian-like detail.
Persian or indigenous?

Marshall and Mortimer Wheeler saw Persian influence (bell capital, polish, Kumrahar hall). Others say the idea of a pillar is Vedic, and the carving tradition was local. Inscriptions in Kharosthi and Aramaic show contact. A balanced view calls it a blend.
Emblem and Ashoka Chakra

The Sarnath capital is national emblem (the bull and horse on the base, “Satyameva Jayate” in Devanagari). The 24-spoke Ashoka Chakra is on the national flag. The 2022 new Parliament’s emblem was a controversy about its lion style. Sarnath Museum holds the original.
How to answer
“Mauryan polish” definition. “Trace the evolution of Indian sculpture from Maurya.” Prelims: which pillar has which animal, location of Barabar caves. Mains: Mauryan art as court and popular streams.
Sangam Literature
Tamilakam’s early voice

Sangam literature is the main source for the first centuries CE in the Tamil south. Prelims asks about the three sangams, anthologies, epics and kings . It also appears in questions on classical languages.
Three sangams

Tradition speaks of three Sangams at Madurai: First (lost), Second at Kapatapuram, Third at Madurai (Pandya patronage). Only the Third survives. Dates: c. 300 BCE to 300 CE (various). Nakkirar, Kapilar, Paranar, Auvaiyar are poets. Tolkappiyam by Tolkappiyar, the oldest Tamil grammar.
Ettuthogai and Pattuppattu

Ettuthogai (Eight Anthologies): Narrinai, Kuruntokai, Ainkurunuru, Patirruppattu, Paripadal, Kalittokai, Akananuru, Purananuru. Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls): Tirumurugarruppadai, Porunararruppadai, Mullaippattu, Pattinappalai, Maduraikkanci, etc. Pathinenkilkanakku : 18 minor works including the Tirukkural by Thiruvalluvar .
Themes: akam and puram

Akam poems are about love (five tinais: kurinji hills, mullai forest, marutham plain, neithal coast, palai desert). Puram poems are about war, kings, charity and public life. The Purananuru praises kings such as Karikala and Nedunjeliyan; Pattinappalai describes Puhar.
The five tinais
Epics

The Five Great Epics: Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal, story of Kovalan, Kannagi, Madhavi), Manimekalai (Sittalai Sattanar, Buddhist), Sivaka Chintamani (Tiruttakkadevar, Jain), Valayapathi, Kundalakesi. Silappadikaram and Manimekalai are the two twin epics; Kannagi worshipped as Pattini in Sri Lanka.
Kings and society

Three dynasties: Cholas (Uraiyur, Puhar; Karikala), Cheras (Vanji; Senguttuvan), Pandyas (Madurai; Nedunjeliyan). Trade with Rome from Muziris, Arikamedu, Puhar. Chieftains (the Velirs) and bards (panar, viralis) received gifts. Brahmins, hero stones (nadukal) and Murugan worship are documented.
Dating and Tamil identity

Scholars disagree on dating. Kamil Zvelebil and K. A. Nilakanta Sastri accept 1st to 3rd century CE for core works. The “Sangam” as an academy is a later tradition. Tamil was given classical language status in 2004, the first language so honoured.
Today

Tirukkural is widely used in public life; a Thiruvalluvar statue stands at Kanyakumari (133 ft). Keezhadi excavations near Madurai, Tamil Nadu, link Sangam-age urban life; the state released results of early dating to the 6th century BCE. Tamil Nadu Archaeology Department runs a site museum there.
How to answer
“Sangam literature is a mirror of society. Discuss.” Prelims: author-work matches (Ilango Adigal, Thiruvalluvar); two Tamil classical dynasties; 2004. Use evidence: poems, Roman gold coins, Keezhadi.
Gupta Science and Mathematics
Classical India’s scientists

The Gupta age is called classical because of science as much as art. Prelims asks who wrote what : Aryabhata, Varahamihira, Brahmagupta, Sushruta, Charaka. Many were from this or the slightly later period.
Aryabhata

Aryabhata (b. 476 CE, Kusumapura; Aryabhatiya, 499 CE) gave the value of pi as 3.1416, explained eclipses by shadows, said the earth rotates on its axis and used place value including zero. Sine tables, solution of linear equations (kuttaka). India’s first satellite (1975) was named after him.
Varahamihira

Court of Chandragupta II or later; Brihat Samhita (weather, architecture, gems), Pancha Siddhantika (five astronomical schools), Brihat Jataka (astrology). He noted that the moon shines by reflected light of the sun.
Brahmagupta and others

Brahmagupta (Brahmasphutasiddhanta, 628 CE; Ujjain) treated zero as a number with rules, negative numbers, gravity as attraction. Later Bhaskara II (Lilavati, 12th century). Zero and decimal system spread via Arabs (Al-Khwarizmi), known as “Arabic numerals”. The Bakhshali manuscript (Pakistan) has a dot for zero (radiocarbon dated by Oxford in 2017 to 3rd or 4th century).
Gupta-era scientists
Medicine

Sushruta Samhita : surgery, rhinoplasty, 100+ instruments. Charaka Samhita : internal medicine, three doshas, attributed to Charaka at Kanishka’s court. Vagbhata’s Ashtanga Hridaya (c. 7th century). Nagarjuna (the alchemist) wrote on metals. Hospitals existed; Fa-Hien saw free charitable dispensaries at Pataliputra.
Metallurgy and technology

The Mehrauli Iron Pillar (Delhi, 4th century, inscription of Chandra, likely Chandragupta II) has resisted rust for 1,600 years because of high phosphorus content and a protective film. A giant copper Buddha was found at Sultanganj (Bihar). Wootz steel developed in the south. Gupta gold coins show excellent minting.
A golden age?

Historians like R. S. Sharma argue the “golden age” label hides rural decline and the rise of land grants. Scientific progress came from a small elite and sometimes borrowed Greek ideas (e.g. Romaka Siddhanta, Yavanajataka). Yet the numerals and zero were original.
Today

ISRO’s Aryabhata satellite (1975) and Bhaskara satellites; Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS) Division at the Ministry of Education; Ayush Ministry promotes Ayurveda; Sushruta is honoured as the “father of surgery” in India. The national space day is on 23 August (Chandrayaan-3 landing, 2023).
How to answer
“Match scientist with book.” “Gupta age was golden age. Critically examine.” Prelims: pi value, zero, Mehrauli pillar. Mains: Contribution of ancient India to science.
Rajputs, Cholas and Regional Kingdoms
India between the Guptas and the Sultans
From the 7th to the 12th century power lay with regional kingdoms. The Cholas built the best local government and a sea empire. Historians argue over “feudalism” and the nature of the state.
The tripartite struggle

For control of Kannauj, three powers fought from the 8th to 10th century: the Gurjara-Pratiharas (west and north), the Palas of Bengal (Dharmapala, Devapala; patrons of Nalanda, Vikramashila) and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan (Dantidurga; Krishna I built Kailasa at Ellora; Amoghavarsha). Arab travellers praised the Rashtrakuta king as one of the great kings of the world.
Rajput states

From the 8th century many clans rose: Chauhans (Ajmer; Prithviraj III lost to Muhammad of Ghor at the Second Battle of Tarain, 1192), Paramaras (Bhoja of Dhar), Chandelas (Khajuraho), Solankis or Chalukyas of Gujarat (Dilwara, Modhera), Gahadavalas (Kannauj), Kalachuris. Features: clan loyalty, forts, land grants, hero stones, patronage of Sanskrit. Mahmud of Ghazni raided from 1000 to 1027 (Somnath, 1025-26); Al-Biruni wrote Kitab-ul-Hind .
Chola rise and empire

Founded by Vijayalaya (c. 850 CE), who took Thanjavur. Rajaraja I (985 to 1014): conquered the Cheras, Pandyas, north Sri Lanka, Maldives; built the Brihadisvara temple. Rajendra I (1014 to 1044): Ganga expedition; Gangaikonda Cholapuram; naval expedition against Srivijaya (c. 1025). Navy and overseas trade with Southeast Asia and China.
Chola administration

Empire divided into mandalams , valanadus , nadus and villages ( ur ). Uttaramerur inscriptions (Parantaka I, 919 and 921 CE): rules for electing village committees by lot ( kudavolai ), with eligibility rules (land, age, learning). Assemblies: ur , sabha (Brahmin villages), nagaram (merchants). Land survey and revenue ( kaniyatchi ); temple as economic centre; devadana , brahmadeya .
Economy, society and culture

Trade guilds: Manigramam, Ayyavole 500, Nanadesi. Iron and textiles; ports: Nagapattinam, Mamallapuram. Society: Brahmins, Vellalas; devadasis . Temples: Brihadisvara, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, Airavatesvara. Bronzes (Nataraja). Literature: Kamban’s Ramavataram , Sekkizhar’s Periya Puranam . Cholas declined after Kulottunga III (13th century) to Pandya and Hoysala.
Other southern and eastern kingdoms

Chalukyas of Badami (Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha, 630; Aihole inscription by Ravikirti), Eastern Chalukyas (Vengi). Pallavas (Mahendravarman I, Narasimhavarman I; Mahabalipuram). Pandyas (Madurai). Hoysalas, Yadavas, Kakatiyas (Warangal; Rani Rudrama Devi). Eastern Gangas (Konark), Palas, Senas.
Indian feudalism and the segmentary state

R. S. Sharma ( Indian Feudalism , 1965) argued that land grants created feudalism and decline of towns after the Guptas. B. D. Chattopadhyaya and others reject it. Burton Stein ( Peasant State and Society in Medieval South India , 1980) proposed the segmentary state : the Chola king had ritual power while local bodies held real power. Others, such as Y. Subbarayalu, point to the strong Chola bureaucracy.
Why it matters today

Uttaramerur is cited as an early example of local democracy and of electoral rules. Cholas’ sea power is part of India’s Indian Ocean narrative; a Chola-style “Sengol” was placed in the new Parliament in 2023 (May). Rajput memory shapes Rajasthan’s heritage tourism and its politics.
How to answer

“Describe the Chola system of local self-government.” “Was early medieval India feudal?” “Tripartite struggle: significance.” Prelims tip: Rajaraja I (Brihadisvara), Rajendra I (Gangaikonda Cholapuram), Uttaramerur (Parantaka I), Second Tarain 1192, Mahmud’s Somnath raid 1025.
Chola Administration
A model of local government

The Imperial Cholas (c. 850 to 1279 CE) built the best-documented early medieval state in the south. UPSC asks about village assemblies, land revenue, army and navy, temple role . The Uttaramerur inscriptions are the star evidence.
Structure of the state

The king ruled with a council of officials. Orders were written by clerks ( olai nayakam ), approved and entered in the records. Titles: Rajaraja I, Rajendra I. Capitals: Thanjavur, then Gangaikondacholapuram. The empire was divided into mandalams (provinces), then valanadus , nadus , and villages ( kurrams or ur ).
Village assemblies

Three bodies: Ur (general village of all taxpayers), Sabha or Mahasabha (brahmadeya, Brahmin villages), Nagaram (merchants’ towns). The Sabha worked through committees called variyams : for tanks, gardens, justice and gold. Members were chosen by kudavolai , a pot-lot system.
Uttaramerur inscriptions

Dated to Parantaka I (c. 919 and 921 CE), they give exact rules: age 35 to 70, own land with tax, own home, knowledge of Vedas and administration, no earlier committee service in last three years, and disqualification for bribery or sins. 30 wards, one member each, chosen by lot with a child drawing the pot-ticket.
Chola territorial units
Revenue and economy

Land revenue, about one-third of produce, was the base; land was surveyed under Rajaraja I and Kulottunga I (1086). Taxes: kadamai (land tax), kudimai (levies). Lands: vellanvagai (peasants), brahmadeya , devadana (temples), pallichandam (Jain). Irrigation: tanks, wells, the Grand Anicut (Kallanai) of Karikala. Guilds like Manigramam and Ayyavole.
Army, navy and temple

Standing army: elephants, cavalry, foot soldiers with regiments; royal bodyguard ( velaikkarar ). A powerful navy raided Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Srivijaya (Rajendra I, 1025). The temple, such as the Brihadisvara, was bank, school, granary and court. Priests, dancers and musicians were paid by temple land.
Segmentary state?

Burton Stein called Chola rule a segmentary state , with a loose centre ritually dominant over self-governing localities. K. A. Nilakanta Sastri argued for a strong, centralised bureaucracy. Newer work sees a layered, flexible state with temple-based legitimacy.
Today

Panchayati raj is often traced to these assemblies. The Chola bronzes and temples (Great Living Chola Temples: Thanjavur 1987, Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram, 2004) are World Heritage. Ancient tanks still serve farmers. The Sengol of the Cholas was placed in the new Parliament in 2023.
How to answer

“Discuss Chola local self-government.” “Compare with the modern panchayat.” Prelims: Uttaramerur, kudavolai, mandalam, Ur and Sabha. Mains structure: Central administration, local assemblies, revenue, military, evaluation.
The Delhi Sultanate
Five dynasties, one state tradition
The Sultanate (1206 to 1526) brought new administration, architecture and an urban economy. UPSC asks for rulers’ reforms and their effects.
Dynasties at a glance

Slave (Mamluk) 1206 to 90: Qutbuddin Aibak, Iltutmish, Raziya, Balban. Khalji 1290 to 1320: Jalaluddin, Alauddin. Tughlaq 1320 to 1414: Ghiyasuddin, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Firoz Shah. Sayyid 1414 to 51; Lodi 1451 to 1526: Bahlol, Sikandar, Ibrahim Lodi. The Sultanate ended with the First Battle of Panipat (1526).
Early Sultans

Iltutmish (1211 to 36): got investiture from the Caliph, introduced the silver tanka and copper jital , the iqta system and the “Corps of Forty” ( Turkan-i-Chahalgani ); Qutb Minar finished. Raziya (1236 to 40): the only woman ruler. Balban (1266 to 87): divine kingship, sijda and paibos , strong spy system ( barids ), crushed the Forty and the Mongols; his court culture was Persian.
Alauddin Khalji (1296 to 1316)

Conquests: Gujarat, Ranthambhor, Chittor, Malwa, and the south under Malik Kafur (Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra, Madurai). Mongol attacks repelled. Market reforms : price controls on grain, cloth, horses, with diwan-i-riyasat and shahna-i-mandi ; to fund a large standing army. Land revenue at half the produce, measured ( masahat ) and direct ( khalisa ) collection; dagh (branding horses) and chehra (muster roll). Chroniclers: Amir Khusrau, Ziauddin Barani.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325 to 51)

Famous “experiments”: (1) capital shift from Delhi to Daulatabad (1327, 1329 return); (2) token currency of brass and copper, which failed because of forgery; (3) taxation increase in the Doab and a famine; (4) the Khurasan and Qarachil plans; (5) agriculture department ( diwan-i-kohi ). Ibn Battuta (Moroccan, visited 1333 to 47) served as a judge. Rebellions began: Bahmani state (1347) and Vijayanagara (1336).
Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351 to 88)

A reformer: new canals (Yamuna to Hisar), towns (Firozabad, Jaunpur, Fatehabad), the tax on Brahmins ( jizya on them too), end of harsh punishments, slave department ( diwan-i-bandagan ), diwan-i-khairat (charity for marriages), and hereditary iqtas. Weak army; fall after his death. Timur’s invasion of Delhi (1398) shattered the Sultanate under Mahmud Tughlaq.
Administration and economy

Sultan with the naib and wazir ; departments: diwan-i-wizarat (finance), diwan-i-arz (army), diwan-i-insha , diwan-i-risalat . Provinces ( iqta , later shiq ), then parganas . Revenue: kharaj , jizya , zakat , khams . A money economy grew; Persian wheel, paper, spinning wheel and new crafts arrived. Cities such as Delhi, Multan and Lahore grew. Sultanate’s Hindu allies and Hindu elites served as revenue collectors.
Was the Sultanate an Islamic state?

Barani saw the state as divinely ordered; the Ulama pressed for sharia. Historians (Mohammad Habib, K. A. Nizami) show that rulers used both Persian kingship and local practice. Irfan Habib stressed the agrarian system and exploitation. Recent writers (Sunil Kumar) highlight a hybrid court. Alauddin’s remark that he ruled by what he thought best for the state is often quoted.
Why it matters today

The Qutb complex, Tughlaqabad, and the Alai Darwaza are heritage sites. The idea of a standardised currency, price control (essential commodities act echoes), and the use of Persian in administration shaped later states. Debates on how to teach this period feed the NCERT and public memory debate.
How to answer

“Assess Alauddin Khalji’s market reforms.” “Was Muhammad bin Tughlaq a mad king or a visionary?” “Why did the Sultanate decline?” Prelims tip: Iltutmish (iqta, tanka), Balban (sijda), Alauddin (market control, dagh), Tughlaq (token currency), Firoz (canals, diwan-i-khairat), Timur 1398.
Vijayanagara and the Bahmanis
The south rises
Two rival states shaped the Deccan for two centuries. UPSC asks about Krishnadevaraya, Hampi’s architecture, the Bahmani administration and the battle of Talikota.
Vijayanagara foundation

Founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty on the Tungabhadra, with the sage Vidyaranya’s support. Four dynasties: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu. Capital Hampi. It was the “bulwark” of Hindu South against the north.
Krishnadevaraya (1509 to 29)

Tuluva dynasty’s greatest king. Defeated Orissa’s Gajapati and Bijapur; built Hazara Rama and Vittala temples; the Ashtadiggajas (eight poets) at court; wrote Amuktamalyada (Telugu). Visitors: Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz (Portuguese) praised Hampi. Allowed Portuguese trade and horses.
Administration and economy

Kings with the mahamandaleswara and nayaks . Nayankara system : military chiefs held land and supplied troops. Ayagar system in villages (twelve officials). Revenue from land and trade. Seaborne trade: horses from Arabia, cloth and spices exported; ports Bhatkal, Mangalore. Temple endowments and irrigation (tanks and canals). Gold coin, the varaha or pagoda .
The Bahmani Sultanate

Founded in 1347 by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah in rebellion against Muhammad bin Tughlaq; capital Gulbarga, later Bidar. Muhammad Gawan , prime minister under Muhammad III, reorganised provinces ( tarafs ), the army and revenue; the Madrasa at Bidar; he was executed in 1481 (nobles’ rivalry: Deccanis vs Afaqis ). Broke up into five: Bijapur (Adil Shah), Golconda (Qutb Shah), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shah), Berar (Imad Shah), Bidar (Barid Shah) by about 1518.
Talikota, 1565

The combined armies of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar defeated Vijayanagara’s Rama Raya at Rakshasa-Tangadi (Talikota) , 1565. Hampi was sacked for months. The empire survived in a smaller form under the Aravidu dynasty at Penukonda and Chandragiri until the 17th century. Reasons: Rama Raya’s overreach in Deccan politics, betrayal by Muslim generals in his army, and the alliance.
Culture and art

Vijayanagara: Hampi (UNESCO, 1986), Vittala temple with the stone chariot, Virupaksha temple, Lotus Mahal (Indo-Islamic). Kannada, Telugu, Tamil and Sanskrit flourished. Bahmani-Deccani: Gol Gumbaz (Bijapur), Golconda Fort, Charminar (Hyderabad, 1591), Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan (Bidar). Dakhni Urdu literature and Deccani painting. Mixed culture both ways.
Hindu kingdom or composite state?

Nineteenth-century writers (Robert Sewell, A Forgotten Empire , 1900) framed it as a Hindu resistance. Later historians (Burton Stein, Phillip Wagoner) note Persianate court dress and titles (“Hindu Sultan”, Hindu Suratrana ) and shared military practice. Richard Eaton ( A Social History of the Deccan ) stresses cultural exchange.
Why it matters today

Hampi is a living site with tourists and temple festivals; its stone chariot appears on the Rs 50 note. The Karnataka–Telangana–Andhra identity draws on both states. Water management at Hampi inspires modern tank restoration. The UNESCO status requires balance between tourism and conservation.
How to answer

“Vijayanagara administration: nayankara system.” “Why did Vijayanagara fall at Talikota?” “Mahmud Gawan’s reforms.” Prelims tip: Harihara-Bukka 1336; Bahmani 1347; Gawan; Krishnadevaraya 1509 to 29; Talikota 1565; Amuktamalyada; Paes and Nuniz.
Delhi Sultanate Administration
How the Sultans ruled

The Sultanate (1206 to 1526) built institutions that Akbar later inherited. UPSC asks about iqta, the army, revenue reforms of Alauddin, central departments and the role of ulema and nobles. Know the Sultan-wise reforms.
The Sultan and the nobles

The Sultan was supreme head, claiming authority from the Caliph (Iltutmish was confirmed by the Abbasid caliph, 1229). Nobility: Turks, later Khaljis, Afghans and Indian Muslims. Balban developed the theory of kingship with sijda and paibos ; Chihalgani (the Forty) were Iltutmish’s nobles, broken by Balban.
Central departments

Wazir (finance; Diwan-i-Wizarat), Ariz-i-mamalik (army; Diwan-i-Arz), Diwan-i-Risalat (religious matters and appeals), Diwan-i-Insha (correspondence). Sadr-us-sudur headed charity. Barid-i-mumalik headed spies. Alauddin set up Diwan-i-Mustakhraj (arrears); Firoz added Diwan-i-Khairat and Diwan-i-Bandagan.
Iqta system

Introduced by Iltutmish : a muqti received revenue of an area (iqta) in place of salary, collected taxes, kept troops and sent surplus. Transfer every few years. Balban checked muqtis; Alauddin reduced their powers; Firoz Tughluq made iqta hereditary; Sikandar Lodi tightened accounts.
Central officers
Alauddin Khalji’s reforms

Standing army paid in cash (dagh, horse branding; chehra, soldier rolls); price control (market controls for grain, cloth, horses, slaves) under the Shahna-i-mandi ; revenue measured land ( masahat ), one-half of produce as kharaj ; tax on houses ( ghari ) and grazing ( chari ). Intermediaries (khuts, muqaddams) were curbed.
Muhammad bin Tughluq and Firoz

Muhammad bin Tughluq tried token coinage, moved the capital to Daulatabad (1327), raised the Doab tax; faced rebellions, and he introduced agricultural loans ( taqavi ). Firoz Tughluq built canals (Hisar), 300 towns, imposed jizya on Brahmins too, abolished some cesses and set up employment bureaus.
Theocracy or secular?

Writers like Ziauddin Barani wanted an Islamic state. Modern historians (Mohammad Habib, K. A. Nizami, Irfan Habib) note a pragmatic state that relied on zawabit (secular regulations) over sharia. Jizya was collected, but rulers rarely demanded religious conversion.
Legacy

Land revenue measurement, mansabdari ancestors (dagh), Persian as court language, the rupee (tanka and silver coin by Sher Shah) and the postal system (dak chowki) all descend from the Sultanate. Modern terms like “Diwan” and “Pargana” remain.
How to answer
“Examine Alauddin Khalji’s market reforms.” “Assess the iqta system.” Prelims: dagh, chehra, jizya, Barani, Ariz-i-mamalik. Mains: Nature of the Sultanate state.
Vijayanagara Art and Architecture
Hampi and a style

Vijayanagara (1336 to 1565) created a distinctive style at Hampi and in Andhra and Tamil Nadu. Questions ask about Hampi monuments, temple features, Krishnadevaraya’s patronage, gopurams and musical pillars . Hampi is a World Heritage Site (1986).
Hampi, the royal centre

Hampi on the Tungabhadra (Karnataka) has two parts: the sacred centre (Virupaksha, Vitthala, Hemakuta) and the royal centre (Lotus Mahal, elephant stables, Mahanavami Dibba, Queen’s bath). Foreign travellers Domingo Paes and Abdur Razzak praised its size and wealth.
Key temples

Virupaksha (Pampapati, Shiva), Vitthala temple (c. 16th century, stone chariot, musical pillars), Hazara Rama temple (a thousand Ramayana panels), Krishna temple built by Krishnadevaraya in 1515, Achyutaraya temple, giant monolithic Narasimha and Ganesha. Veerabhadra at Lepakshi (Andhra).
Architectural features

Blended Dravida with Deccani Islamic style. Features: tall raya gopurams (Krishnadevaraya’s gateways at Kalahasti, Kanchi, Chidambaram, Tiruvannamalai), kalyana mandapas (marriage halls with composite pillars), amman shrines for goddess, pillared corridors , horse-rearing pillars with rearing yalis, and Indo-Islamic arches in secular buildings like the Lotus Mahal.
Hampi complexes
Sculpture and painting

Large bas-reliefs and dwarapalas, yali pillars, Bhakti-themed bronzes (Krishnadevaraya and his queens, Tirumala). Lepakshi murals in the Veerabhadra temple are major Vijayanagara paintings. Dance and music were patronised, and Telugu literature flourished (Krishnadevaraya’s Amuktamalyada, the Ashtadiggajas).
Water and fortification

Hampi’s canals, stepped tanks and aqueducts were fed from the Tungabhadra by anicuts (Turtha canal). Fortification walls and gates enclosed the city in seven lines (Paes). Defeat at Talikota (1565) led to its sack, leaving the present ruins.
Indo-Islamic influence

George Michell and others note Deccani influence in secular buildings, while temples stay Dravidian. Some argue Vijayanagara’s architecture is pure “Hindu empire”; others see it as a composite culture. “Sewell’s A Forgotten Empire” (1900) popularised the site.
Today

Hampi (Group of Monuments at Hampi, UNESCO 1986) draws tourists; the Hampi Utsav and the Vijayanagara empire’s 650th-year events recall it. ASI and the Hampi World Heritage Area Management Authority protect it. Lepakshi (Andhra) is on the tentative list; the Basavanna bull is a major attraction.
How to answer
“Vijayanagara temple architecture and Dravida synthesis.” Prelims: Vitthala temple, Hazara Rama, Lotus Mahal, Lepakshi. Mains: Evaluate Krishnadevaraya as patron of art and literature.
The Mughal Empire: Polity and Administration
The great early modern empire
The Mughals ruled most of India for about 180 years at their peak. Administration (mansabdari, revenue) and culture are tested every year.
Establishment

Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) , Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527), Afghans at Ghaghra (1529). Humayun lost to Sher Shah at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540), returned in 1555. Sher Shah Suri (1540 to 45): Grand Trunk Road, rupiya , dam , a revenue system based on measurement, and sarais . Humayun’s regaining of Delhi in 1555.
Akbar (1556 to 1605)

Second Battle of Panipat (1556) with Bairam Khan. Conquests: Malwa, Gondwana, Chittor (1568), Gujarat, Bengal, Kashmir, Kandahar, Khandesh. Religious policy: abolished the pilgrim tax (1563) and jizya (1564); Ibadat Khana (1575); mahzar (1579); Din-i-Ilahi (1582); sulh-i-kul (peace with all). Court: Abul Fazl, Faizi, Todar Mal, Birbal, Tansen, Man Singh. Rajput alliance.
Mansabdari system

Mansab = rank. Two numbers: zat (personal rank and pay) and sawar (cavalry to be kept). Ranks from 10 to 10,000 (princes higher). Paid by jagirs (revenue assignments) or cash; dagh and chehra continued. Transferable and non-hereditary. Under Shah Jahan, the month scale ( masik ) and sihbandi . The jagirdari crisis under Aurangzeb (shortage of jagirs) is linked by Satish Chandra to the decline.
Land revenue and economy

Todar Mal ’s zabt (Akbar’s Dahsala , 1580): measured land, average prices and yields of ten years, revenue in cash (about one-third of produce). Other systems: batai , kankut , nasaq . Crops: wheat, rice, cotton, indigo, sugarcane; new: tobacco, maize, chillies. Trade with Europeans brought silver. Cities: Agra, Lahore, Surat. Craft: cotton textiles of Bengal and Gujarat. The zamindars were intermediaries.
Central and provincial administration

Emperor ( Padshah ), Wakil , Diwan-i-Kul (finance), Mir Bakhshi (army), Sadr-us-Sudur (religious grants), Mir Saman (household), Qazi-ul-Quzat (justice). 12 subas by Akbar, later more; Subadar , Diwan , Bakhshi , Faujdar , Kotwal . Sarkars and parganas; Amil and qanungo . A centralised system with checks.
Later Mughals

Jahangir (1605 to 27): chain of justice, Nur Jahan’s role, painting; Sir Thomas Roe’s embassy (1615). Shah Jahan (1628 to 58): Taj Mahal, new city Shahjahanabad; war of succession (1657 to 58). Aurangzeb (1658 to 1707): reimposed jizya (1679), temple controversies, Deccan campaigns (Bijapur 1686, Golconda 1687), revolts of Jats, Satnamis, Sikhs (Guru Tegh Bahadur’s execution 1675), Marathas, Rajputs; the Deccan ulcer.
Why did the Mughal Empire decline?

Irfan Habib ( Agrarian System of Mughal India ) stresses an agrarian crisis from heavy revenue demands. Satish Chandra points to the jagirdari crisis. M. Athar Ali emphasises the growth of the nobility. Others (Jadunath Sarkar) blamed Aurangzeb’s religious policy; modern scholars (Muzaffar Alam, C. A. Bayly, Chetan Singh) point to regional powers rising and the shift of power to provinces. Balanced answers use several causes.
Why it matters today

The Mughal revenue records ( Ain-i-Akbari ), the idea of an empire-wide administration and the language Urdu (Hindustani) are living legacies. The Grand Trunk Road survives as NH 1 and NH 2. Debates about historical figures in textbooks and place names make the Mughals a political subject. The Red Fort is the site of Independence Day.
How to answer

“Mansabdari system: features and problems.” “Was Akbar’s religious policy a political strategy?” “Causes of the decline of the Mughal Empire.” Prelims tip: Panipat 1526, 1556; Chausa 1539; Khanwa 1527; Haldighati 1576; Dahsala 1580; zat and sawar; Ain-i-Akbari (Abul Fazl).
Marathas and the Decline of the Mughals
The challengers
The Marathas, Sikhs and regional nawabs filled the space left by the Mughals. They matter to the story of how the British found it easy to expand.
Rise of Shivaji

Shivaji (1630 to 1680), son of Shahaji Bhonsle, took Torna (1646) and built Raigad. Killed Afzal Khan (1659). Attacked Surat (1664); Treaty of Purandar (1665) with Jai Singh; visited Aurangzeb at Agra (1666) and escaped. Coronation at Raigad (1674) as Chhatrapati. Southern campaign (Jinji, Vellore, 1677 to 78).
Shivaji’s administration

Ashtapradhan : Peshwa (prime minister), Amatya, Mantri, Sachiv, Sumant, Senapati, Pandit Rao, Nyayadhish. Revenue: ryotwari -like, with chauth (one-fourth) and sardeshmukhi (extra one-tenth) from neighbouring territory. Salaried army, strong forts, navy (Kanhoji Angre later). Reduced the role of deshmukhs and abolished jagirs. Hill forts and guerrilla war ( ganimi kava ).
After Shivaji

Sambhaji executed in 1689; Rajaram; Tarabai. Shahu was released in 1707; civil war with Tarabai; Treaty of Warna (1731) split Kolhapur and Satara. Peshwas from Balaji Vishwanath (1713 to 20) took control: Baji Rao I (1720 to 40), Balaji Baji Rao (1740 to 61). Maratha confederacy: Scindia (Gwalior), Holkar (Indore), Bhonsle (Nagpur), Gaekwad (Baroda). Raids reached Delhi, Orissa, the south.
Panipat 1761 and after

At the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated the Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau and Vishwasrao. About 100,000 died. It broke Maratha reach and weakened the north. Mahadji Scindia revived their power; Nana Phadnavis in Pune. Three Anglo-Maratha wars: 1775 to 82 (Treaty of Salbai), 1803 to 05, 1817 to 18, ending Maratha power.
Mughal decline and successor states

After Aurangzeb (1707) came weak rulers. Nadir Shah sacked Delhi (1739; took the Peacock Throne). Abdali’s raids. Successor states: Bengal (Murshid Quli Khan), Awadh (Saadat Khan), Hyderabad (Nizam-ul-Mulk, 1724), Rohillas, Jats (Suraj Mal), Sikhs (Ranjit Singh later), Mysore (Haidar Ali), Travancore (Marthanda Varma). The Mughal emperor became a figurehead; Shah Alam II.
Sikhs and Jats

Guru Nanak, Guru Arjan (Adi Granth, 1604; killed 1606), Guru Hargobind, Guru Tegh Bahadur, Guru Gobind Singh (Khalsa, 1699; died 1708). Banda Bahadur’s rebellion (1709 to 1716). Misls in the 18th century; Ranjit Singh (1799 to 1839) unified the Punjab, the Sikh Empire. The Jats (Gokula, Raja Ram, Churaman, Suraj Mal at Bharatpur).
Who is to blame for decline?

Jadunath Sarkar blamed Aurangzeb; Marxist writers (Irfan Habib) blamed the jagirdari and agrarian crisis. Revisionists (Chetan Singh, Muzaffar Alam, C. A. Bayly) see an 18th-century of regional growth and new prosperity, not a dark age. On the Marathas, Grant Duff praised Shivaji; Govind Sakharam Sardesai and Jadunath Sarkar both studied them. Was Shivaji a Hindu or a national king? Historians (Satish Chandra) say a regional ruler with secular practice, including Muslims in the army.
Why it matters today

Shivaji is a regional and national icon; Maharashtra’s politics uses his memory (statue and memorial debates). The Khalsa and Gurdwara reform shape Sikh identity; Ranjit Singh’s legacy is a Punjab emblem. Federal power-sharing between the centre and regional power has roots in this age. Indian Navy’s new ensign (2022) draws on Shivaji’s seal.
How to answer

“Assess Shivaji’s administration.” “Why did the Marathas fail to build an all-India empire?” “Eighteenth century India: dark age or transition?” Prelims tip: Panipat 1761; Ashtapradhan; chauth and sardeshmukhi; Nadir Shah 1739; Khalsa 1699; Hyderabad 1724; Treaty of Purandar 1665.
Mughal Architecture
A tested evolution
Mughal architecture is a staple of Prelims. The question is usually who built what, material, and features . Track the path from red sandstone (Akbar) to white marble (Shah Jahan).
Babur and Humayun

Babur built mosques at Panipat (Kabuli Bagh) and Sambhal and gardens (charbagh). Humayun’s Tomb , Delhi (1565–72, built by Haji Begum, Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas): first garden-tomb, red sandstone with white marble; double dome; UNESCO site 1993. Sher Shah built the Qila-i-Kuhna and his tomb at Sasaram, an octagonal tomb on a lake.
Akbar

Red sandstone, fusion with Hindu and Gujarati styles. Agra Fort ; Fatehpur Sikri (1571–85): Buland Darwaza (1576, victory over Gujarat), Jama Masjid, Diwan-i-Khas, Panch Mahal, Jodha Bai’s palace, Salim Chishti’s tomb in white marble; Akbar’s tomb at Sikandra (Agra). Fatehpur Sikri was abandoned due to water shortage.
Jahangir and Nur Jahan

Itimad-ud-Daulah’s tomb (Agra, 1622–28, by Nur Jahan): first Mughal building entirely in white marble with pietra dura inlay (parchin kari); sometimes called the “baby Taj”. Gardens: Shalimar Bagh and Nishat Bagh, Kashmir. Jahangir’s tomb at Lahore.
Evolution
Shah Jahan

The golden age of Mughal architecture: Taj Mahal (1632–53, Ustad Ahmad Lahori; double dome, minarets, four-part charbagh; UNESCO 1983), Red Fort and Jama Masjid in Delhi, Moti Masjid in Agra, Diwan-i-Aam and Khas (“If there is a paradise on earth…”), Shalimar Bagh Lahore, Peacock Throne. The city Shahjahanabad (1648).
Aurangzeb and decline

Badshahi Mosque (Lahore, 1673), Moti Masjid in the Red Fort, and Bibi ka Maqbara (Aurangabad), a weak copy of the Taj built by his son Azam Shah. Royal patronage declined, but regional Mughal styles flowered in Awadh (Bara Imambara, Lucknow) and the Deccan.
Persian or Indian?

Features are Persian (charbagh, iwan, double dome, pietra dura) but craftsmen and motifs are Indian (chhatris, jharokhas, brackets, lotus). Percy Brown called it a synthesis. Gardens symbolised paradise; the Taj plan shows the river-side garden, unlike the usual tomb at the centre.
Today

The Taj Mahal, Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri, Humayun’s Tomb and Red Fort are UNESCO sites. Taj Trapezium Zone rules limit pollution near the Taj (M. C. Mehta case, 1996). The Red Fort hosts the Independence Day speech; it was taken up under the “Adopt a Heritage” scheme (2017).
How to answer
“Trace evolution of Mughal architecture.” Prelims: first garden tomb (Humayun’s), first marble (Itimad), Buland Darwaza. Mains: Mughal synthesis in architecture, with examples.
Maratha Administration
Shivaji’s state-building

Shivaji (crowned 1674) built a compact, centralised, tax-based state. UPSC asks about the Ashta Pradhan, chauth and sardeshmukhi, forts, navy and the Peshwa period . It also appears with the Maratha Military Landscapes World Heritage listing.
Rise and coronation

Shivaji, born 1630 at Shivneri to Shahaji and Jijabai, took Torna (1646), killed Afzal Khan (1659), fought Shaista Khan (1663), signed the Treaty of Purandar (1665) and escaped from Agra (1666). He was crowned at Raigad on 6 June 1674 by Gaga Bhatt as Chhatrapati , and died in 1680.
Ashta Pradhan

A council of eight ministers, with no hereditary posts: Peshwa (prime minister), Amatya (finance), Mantri (the king’s records), Sachiv (correspondence), Sumant (foreign affairs), Senapati (commander-in-chief), Pandit Rao (religion, charity), Nyayadhish (justice). Ministers were advisers, not independent. Many held military commands.
Revenue

Based on Malik Ambar’s ryotwari-type system with measurement by rod ( kathi ); cultivators paid directly to officials, not jagirdars. Shivaji abolished the role of hereditary deshmukhs. Chauth (one-fourth of revenue) and Sardeshmukhi (an additional 10 per cent) were levied on neighbouring non-Maratha areas, and in return protection was offered.
Ashta Pradhan
Army, forts and navy

Cavalry were paga (regular, paid by the state) and silahdar (irregular, own horses). Infantry were the mavli . Forts: Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Sindhudurg, with three officers sharing power (havaldar, sabnis, karkhanis). The navy at Kolaba and Sindhudurg under Kanhoji Angre later. Guerrilla war ( ganimi kava ).
Peshwa and confederacy

After Shahu (1707 to 1749), power passed to the Peshwas of Pune: Balaji Vishwanath (Treaty of 1719), Baji Rao I (1720 to 40), Balaji Baji Rao (Nanasaheb), who lost the Third Battle of Panipat (1761). A confederacy of Scindia (Gwalior), Holkar (Indore), Gaekwad (Baroda), Bhonsle (Nagpur) grew. The Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775–1818) ended it.
Hindu swaraj or a revenue state?

Nationalist historians such as G. S. Sardesai and Ranade praised Shivaji as a national hero. Marxists note a revenue-extracting state with peasant misery. Jadunath Sarkar was critical but also admiring. Debate also exists on whether he was a Hindu-nationalist or inclusive (he employed Muslims in his army and navy).
Today

In July 2025 UNESCO inscribed the Maratha Military Landscapes of India (12 forts, including Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Sindhudurg and Gingee) as a World Heritage Site. Shivaji’s coronation anniversary is a Maharashtra festival. The Indian Navy’s emblem was redesigned in 2022 inspired by Shivaji’s seal.
How to answer
“Examine Shivaji’s administration.” Prelims: Ashta Pradhan names, Chauth, Treaty of Purandar, Raigad. Mains: How far was the Maratha state different from the Mughal?
The Sikh Gurus
Faith, politics and a state

The ten Gurus built a distinct faith, scripture and later a political power. Prelims asks about each Guru’s contribution and Mughal confrontations. It links with Bhakti and the Punjab freedom struggle.
Guru Nanak (1469–1539)

Born at Talwandi (Nankana Sahib). Taught Ik Onkar , equality, naam japna, kirat karna, vand chakna . Founded Kartarpur (on the Ravi), started langar . Rejected caste, idols, asceticism. Four udasis (journeys). Succeeded by Angad.
Gurus 2 to 4

Angad (2nd) devised Gurmukhi script. Amar Das (3rd) institutionalised langar, set up manjis, opposed sati and purdah; Akbar visited him. Ram Das (4th) founded Amritsar (land from Akbar) and the Harmandir sarovar, started the masand system. The Guruship became hereditary after him.
Arjan Dev (5th)

Compiled the Adi Granth (1604) with verses of Gurus, Kabir, Ravidas, Farid. Completed the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) in 1604, founded Tarn Taran and Kartarpur (Jalandhar). Executed in 1606 under Jahangir (supporting Khusrau). Considered the first martyr.
Hargobind and Tegh Bahadur

Hargobind (6th) wore two swords ( miri and piri ), built the Akal Takht , fought Mughal forces. Har Rai (7th) and Har Krishan (8th; child Guru). Tegh Bahadur (9th) founded Anandpur Sahib; he was executed at Delhi in 1675 under Aurangzeb for defending Kashmiri Pandits’ right to worship (Gurdwara Sis Ganj).
The ten Gurus
Guru Gobind Singh (10th)

On Baisakhi 1699 at Anandpur he founded the Khalsa with the Panj Pyare and the Five Ks (kesh, kangha, kara, kirpan, kachera). Surname Singh and Kaur. Battles at Bhangani and Chamkaur. Composed the Dasam Granth; ended the line of living Gurus, declaring the Guru Granth Sahib to be Guru (1708, Nanded). Banda Singh Bahadur led the next phase.
After the Gurus

Banda Singh Bahadur (1708 to 1716) captured Sirhind. Misls (12 confederacies) and then Maharaja Ranjit Singh (r. 1799 to 1839) built the Sikh Empire from Lahore, with the Anglo-Sikh wars (1845–46; 1848–49) ending it. The Singh Sabha (1873) and Akali movement (Gurdwara Reform Act, 1925; SGPC) followed.
Faith or politics?

W. H. McLeod argued that early Sikhism was a movement of the Sant tradition (like Kabir), that later became militant. Others (Harbans Singh) stress continuity of spiritual-political thought from Nanak. The sources for the early period are also debated.
Today

The Kartarpur Corridor (Gurdaspur to Pakistan’s Kartarpur Sahib) opened in November 2019 for Guru Nanak’s 550th birth anniversary. Veer Bal Diwas is observed on 26 December for the Sahibzade.
