The Golden Temple’s langar serves tens of thousands daily. Punjabi in Gurmukhi is a constitutional language.
How to answer
“Evolution of the Sikh religion from Nanak to Gobind Singh.” Prelims: Arjan, Adi Granth, Khalsa 1699, Five Ks, Akal Takht. Mains: Relationship of Sikh Gurus and Mughals.
Bhakti and Sufi Traditions
Faith that crossed boundaries
Bhakti and Sufism are the main strands of medieval religious life. They shaped language, music and social ideas. UPSC asks for saints, teachings and effects.
Origins of Bhakti

Bhakti (devotion) began in the south with the Alvars (Vishnu) and Nayanars (Shiva), between the 6th and 9th centuries, who sang in Tamil and welcomed women and low castes (Andal, Karaikkal Ammaiyar). Texts: Nalayira Divya Prabandham , Tevaram . Later: Shankara’s Advaita (8th c.), Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita, 11th to 12th c.), Madhva (Dvaita), Basavanna’s Lingayat movement (Karnataka, 12th c.; Anubhava Mandapa).
Bhakti in the north

Ramananda (14th to 15th c.): Rama bhakti; disciples include Kabir and Ravidas. Kabir : nirguna God, attacked idol worship and caste; Bijak. Guru Nanak : one God, equality, langar , sangat . Chaitanya (Bengal): Krishna bhakti, kirtan . Tulsidas ( Ramcharitmanas ), Surdas , Mirabai , Raskhan . Vallabhacharya (Pushtimarga).
Maharashtra and the east

Varkari tradition : Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram, Janabai; Pandharpur and Vitthal. Sankaradeva (Assam, Ekasarana dharma ), Shrimanta Sankardeva ’s Namghar and Borgeet . Others: Narsi Mehta (Gujarat), Chandidas (Bengal), Annamacharya (Andhra). Many saints came from low castes and used the vernacular.
Sufism

Sufism is the mystical stream of Islam, stressing love and union with God. Orders ( silsilas ): Chishti (Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer; Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi; Baba Farid), Suhrawardi (Multan, Bahauddin Zakariya), Qadiri , Naqshbandi (Sirhindi, who opposed Akbar’s liberalism). Practices: khanqah , sama (music), langar . Chishtis kept away from the state; Suhrawardis accepted it.
Common ground and expression

Both movements used local languages: Kabir and Tulsi in Hindi, Dnyaneshwar in Marathi, Sufis in Dakhni and Hindavi (Amir Khusrau, Baba Farid in Punjabi). The Chishtis of Ajmer and Delhi attracted Hindu and Muslim devotees. Sufi poets such as Jayasi ( Padmavat ) and Rahim. Qawwali and bhajan, Kabir panth and Sikhism came from them. Both rejected rigid orthodoxy.
Social impact

They challenged caste, ritual and priestly control; spread vernacular literature; gave women a voice (Mirabai, Lalla Ded). They brought communities closer and helped shape the ganga-jamuni tehzeeb . Yet they did not abolish caste; many movements later formed new sects or castes. Akbar’s sulh-i-kul was nurtured in this air.
Social revolt or spiritual reform?

Historians (Satish Chandra, Irfan Habib) see Bhakti as a response to a changing society and urban craft groups; Marxists tied it to peasants and artisans. Others (Romila Thapar) view it as a religious expression within a plural society. Scholars debate the term “movement”, as the saints were not organised. On Sufis, Richard Eaton ( Sufis of Bijapur ) studies state ties.
Why it matters today

Kabir’s and Mirabai’s verses are in school books and music. The dargah of Ajmer, with a huge urs, draws all faiths. Pandharpur’s wari draws lakhs. Discussion on communal harmony cites these traditions; recent controversies over dargahs and temples revisit it. The Sikh langar became a symbol of free community kitchens worldwide.
How to answer

“Bhakti and Sufi movements promoted social harmony. Discuss.” “Compare the teachings of Kabir and Guru Nanak.” Prelims tip: Alvars = Vishnu; Nayanars = Shiva; Ramanuja = Vishishtadvaita; Basavanna = Lingayat; Chishti = Ajmer, Nizamuddin; Suhrawardi = Multan.
Bhakti Saints in Depth
Individual saints, not just ideas

The existing lesson covers the movement. Here we learn each saint, region and message , because Prelims matches names to ideas. The Bhakti movement spread from the Tamil south in a long chain of saints.
The Tamil roots

Alvars (12 Vaishnava poets; Andal, Nammalvar, Periyalvar), whose verses are compiled in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham . Nayanars (63 Shaiva saints; Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar, Manikkavachakar), compiled in the Tirumurai by Nambiyandar Nambi. Both rejected caste barriers and used Tamil.
Acharyas and philosophy

Shankara (Advaita, 8th century, Kaladi). Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita, 11th to 12th century; Sri Bhashya). Madhva (Dvaita, Udupi). Nimbarka (Dvaitadvaita), Vallabhacharya (Pushtimarg, Shuddhadvaita). Ramananda (Varanasi, 14th century) took Bhakti north, with disciples including Kabir, Ravidas and Sena the barber.
Nirguna saints

Kabir (15th century; Bijak, Sakhi, Ramaini): formless God, rejected idol worship and caste, both Hindu and Muslim ritual; weaver of Varanasi. Guru Nanak and Dadu Dayal (Rajasthan). Ravidas (cobbler, Varanasi; Mirabai’s guru in tradition). Languages were Hindi dialects. Compiled in the Granth.
Regional Bhakti voices
Saguna saints in the north

Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas, Awadhi, c. 1574), Surdas (Sur Sagar, Braj, Krishna), Mirabai (Krishna devotee, Mewar), Chaitanya (Bengal, kirtan, Gaudiya Vaishnavism), Narsinh Mehta (Gujarat, “Vaishnav Jan To”). Sankaradeva (Assam) founded Ek Sarana Dharma and the sattra institution, plus Borgeet and Ankia Naat.
Maharashtra and Karnataka

Dnyaneshwar (Dnyaneshwari, a Marathi commentary on the Gita, 1290), Namdev , Eknath , Tukaram (abhangas), Chokhamela and Janabai: Varkari panth centred on Vitthala of Pandharpur . Basavanna (12th century, Kalyana) founded Veerashaivism with vachanas , the Anubhava Mantapa, rejecting caste and ritual.
Social revolution or accommodation?

Some see Bhakti as a challenge to caste and Brahmin ritual (Kabir, Ravidas). Others, like Romila Thapar, see it as often absorbed into the existing structure; many saints still accepted varna. Irfan Habib links it to artisan and peasant protest against feudal order. Interaction with Sufism is another thread.
Today

Pandharpur’s Ashadhi Wari pilgrimage draws lakhs of Warkaris every year. Sant Kabir Jayanti and Tulsi Jayanti are celebrated. Bhakti poetry shaped modern Hindi, Marathi and Assamese. The Statue of Equality (216 ft, Hyderabad, 2022) honours Ramanuja.
How to answer
“Bhakti saints promoted social equality. Examine.” “Compare Kabir and Nanak.” Prelims: Alvars vs Nayanars, Ramananda’s disciples, Sankaradeva, Basavanna.
Temple Architecture: Nagara, Dravida, Vesara
Stone as history
Temples are the best-preserved record of Indian kings, faith and craft. UPSC asks for style features, dynasties and examples, often with a UNESCO angle.
Parts of a temple

Garbhagriha (sanctum), mandapa (hall), shikhara or vimana (tower), antarala (vestibule), amalaka (ribbed disc on Nagara tower), kalasha (finial). Early Gupta temples (Deogarh Dashavatara, Bhitargaon brick temple) set the pattern. The three broad styles are described in the Vastu texts: Nagara (north), Dravida (south), Vesara (Deccan mix).
Nagara style

Found from the Himalayas to the Vindhyas. Features: a curved shikhara ( rekha-deula or latina type), temple on a raised platform, no boundary wall or large gateway. Sub-schools: Odisha (Lingaraja, Bhubaneswar; Konark Sun Temple; Jagannath, Puri; deul and jagamohana), Khajuraho (Chandela, Kandariya Mahadeva, c. 1000 CE; panchayatana plan), Solanki (Modhera Sun Temple, Gujarat, 1026), Dilwara Jain temples (Mount Abu).
Dravida style

The tower is a stepped pyramid, vimana , with a rectangular compound wall and a large gopuram at the gateway. A water tank and pillared halls are common. Dynasties: Pallavas (Mahabalipuram Shore Temple, Kanchi Kailasanatha), Cholas (Brihadisvara, Thanjavur, built by Rajaraja I about 1010 CE; Gangaikonda Cholapuram; Airavatesvara, Darasuram), Pandyas and Nayakas (Madurai Meenakshi, large gopurams).
Vesara and other styles

Vesara is the mixed style of the Deccan. Chalukyas of Badami and Aihole (Durga temple, Virupaksha at Pattadakal), Rashtrakutas (Kailasa at Ellora, carved from one rock under Krishna I), Hoysalas (Belur, Halebid, Somnathpur; star-shaped plan on a platform, soapstone, called jagati ). Others: Kashmir (Martand Sun Temple, Karkota), Himachal (wooden temples), Kerala (sloping roofs), Assam (Kamakhya).
Rock-cut and monolithic

Barabar caves (Mauryan, polished). Kanheri, Karle. Elephanta (Shiva, Maharashtra). The Kailasa temple at Ellora is carved top down from a single rock. Pallava monolithic rathas at Mahabalipuram (Narasimhavarman I Mamalla). Ajanta and Ellora combine Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves.
How strict are the labels?

The Nagara-Dravida-Vesara scheme is helpful but not sharp: Odisha and Khajuraho differ from each other, and the Deccan mixed both. Scholars such as Adam Hardy speak of a “Karnata Dravida” tradition. Still, for exams, learn the three types and exceptions.
Why it matters today

Great Living Chola Temples (Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, Darasuram), Khajuraho, Konark, Mahabalipuram, Pattadakal, Hampi and the Hoysala temples are UNESCO World Heritage sites (the Hoysala group was added in 2023). The Ram temple at Ayodhya (consecrated January 2024) is built in the Nagara style. Temple economy and the HR&CE laws in states raise legal debates.
How to answer

“Distinguish between Nagara and Dravida architecture.” Use a two-column table. “Chola temple architecture was a mirror of imperial power.” Prelims tip: gopuram = Dravida; shikhara with amalaka = Nagara; star plan = Hoysala; Kailasa at Ellora = Rashtrakuta.
Buddhist, Indo-Islamic and Colonial Architecture
Layers of one building tradition
Stupas, mosques, forts and Victorian railway stations are all part of the same story. UPSC wants you to date them and to name the style.
Buddhist architecture

Stupa : relic mound. Parts: anda (dome), harmika , chhatra , vedika , torana . Sanchi (Ashoka, later enlarged under Shungas and Satavahanas; torana gates), Bharhut, Amaravati, Sarnath (Dhamek). Chaityas (prayer halls) and viharas (monasteries): Karle chaitya, Ajanta, Bhaja. Ashokan pillars with lion capitals (Sarnath; national emblem).
Delhi Sultanate architecture

Introduced the arch, dome, minaret and lime mortar, using the true arch . Phases: Slave (Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, Qutb Minar, Adhai Din ka Jhonpra, Ajmer), Khalji (Alai Darwaza, Siri), Tughlaq (Tughlaqabad; sloping walls, Firozshah Kotla), Sayyid-Lodi (octagonal tombs, Lodi Garden). Provincial: Jaunpur (Atala Masjid), Gujarat (Jama Masjid, Ahmedabad; Sidi Saiyyed jali), Bengal, Malwa (Hoshang Shah’s tomb), Bijapur (Gol Gumbaz, with a very large dome).
Mughal architecture

Babur : gardens. Humayun’s tomb (Delhi, 1560s, Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas; first garden-tomb, charbagh). Akbar : Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri (Buland Darwaza, Jodha Bai palace, Panch Mahal; red sandstone), Akbar’s tomb at Sikandra. Jahangir : Itimad-ud-daula (Nur Jahan; first use of white marble and pietra dura ). Shah Jahan : Taj Mahal (1632 to 1653, Ustad Ahmad Lahori), Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Moti Masjid. Aurangzeb : Bibi ka Maqbara, Badshahi Mosque, Lahore.
Regional and Rajput forts

Rajput forts: Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Amber, Jaisalmer, Mehrangarh. Hill Forts of Rajasthan are UNESCO sites (2013). Deccan: Golconda, Daulatabad. Vijayanagara: Hampi (Vittala temple stone chariot; Lotus Mahal; Indo-Islamic mix). Sikh: Golden Temple, Amritsar (Guru Arjan Dev; Harmandir Sahib). The Sultanate and Mughal forms blended with local craft: the chhatri , jharokha and jali are Indian elements.
Colonial architecture

Early : Portuguese and French churches (Basilica of Bom Jesus, Goa), Danish Tranquebar. Classical : Fort William (Calcutta), Government House. Indo-Saracenic : Gateway of India, Victoria Memorial, Madras High Court (Robert Chisholm, F. W. Stevens). Gothic : Victoria Terminus (Mumbai), University of Mumbai. Imperial Delhi : Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker, New Delhi (1911 to 1931), Rashtrapati Bhavan, India Gate.
Modern after 1947

Le Corbusier’s Chandigarh (Capitol Complex is a UNESCO site since 2016); Louis Kahn (IIM Ahmedabad); Charles Correa (Gandhi Smarak, Jawahar Kala Kendra); Laurie Baker’s low-cost homes; B. V. Doshi (Pritzker 2018). The new Parliament building was inaugurated in May 2023 as part of the Central Vista project.
Was Indo-Saracenic respectful or political?

Thomas Metcalf ( An Imperial Vision , 1989) argued that Indo-Saracenic was a style of empire: British rulers used Indian forms to show themselves as heirs to Mughals. Others stress craftsmanship by Indian workers and the hybrid creativity. The Central Vista debate echoes the old question of how power uses architecture.
Why it matters today

The Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Qutb Minar, Humayun’s Tomb, Sanchi, Rani ki Vav (Gujarat), Victorian Gothic and Art Deco of Mumbai (2018) and Ahmedabad (2017, India’s first World Heritage City) show a living urban heritage. Conservation, ASI protected monuments and the Ancient Monuments Act 1958 are all in the news.
How to answer

“Mughal architecture synthesised Persian and Indian elements. Discuss.” “Indo-Saracenic architecture—what and why?” Prelims tip: Humayun’s tomb (charbagh), Itimad-ud-daula (pietra dura), Buland Darwaza (Akbar), Gol Gumbaz (Bijapur), Delhi Gate and India Gate (Lutyens).
Sculpture: Mauryan to Chola Bronzes
Stone and metal that speak
Each period of Indian sculpture has a signature look. Prelims asks you to match a school with its features and its material.
Indus and Mauryan

Harappan : bearded priest (steatite), dancing girl (bronze, lost-wax), seals. Mauryan : polished sandstone, Chunar. Court art: Ashokan pillars and lion capital from Sarnath; Didarganj Yakshi; Dhauli elephant. Folk art: Parkham Yaksha (Mathura), Yakshis and Yakshas.
Post-Mauryan schools

Gandhara (Kushana): Greco-Roman influence, Buddha with wavy hair, drapery, grey schist. Mathura : indigenous, red sandstone, first Buddha figures as well as Jain and Hindu figures; Kanishka’s headless statue. Amaravati (Satavahana): white marble, narrative friezes with the body shown as flowing. Bharhut and Sanchi reliefs show aniconic Buddha (wheel, tree, footprints).
Gupta and post-Gupta

Classical grace and calm. Sarnath Buddha in teaching pose ( dharmachakra mudra ); Mathura standing Buddha; Sultanganj copper Buddha. Hindu icons: Vishnu at Deogarh, Varaha at Udayagiri. After the Guptas: Pala (Bengal, black basalt, bronze at Nalanda), Pratihara and Chandela.
Pallava and Chalukya sculpture

Mahabalipuram: Descent of the Ganga (Arjuna’s Penance) , a huge relief on a rock face; Mahishasuramardini cave. Elephanta (Trimurti, Shiva). Badami and Aihole (Chalukya). Ellora: Ravana shaking Kailasa. Natural movement and balance in all these.
Chola bronzes

Cast by the lost-wax (cire perdue) method, an old Indian process. A clay model is covered in wax, then in clay again, wax is melted out, and metal is poured in. The Cholas (9th to 13th centuries) made the most famous bronzes: Nataraja (Shiva as cosmic dancer, ring of flames), Shiva as Ardhanarishvara, Sivakami, Rama, Sita, Hanuman, Parvati. The Swamimalai artisans (the sthapathis ) still follow the old method.
Reading a Nataraja

The raised right hand holds the damaru (creation), the left holds fire (destruction). Another right hand makes abhaya (fear not); the left points to the raised foot (release). He dances on the dwarf Apasmara , the demon of ignorance. The ring of fire is the cosmos. The image became a symbol of Indian art; a Nataraja statue stands at CERN, Geneva (2004).
Gandhara: borrowed or reborn?

Western scholars once called it “Greco-Buddhist” and the high point of Indian Buddhist art. Indian nationalists such as Coomaraswamy argued the Mathura school was truly Indian and older in iconography. Today most see both as parallel responses to patronage in the Kushana world. For exams: keep the contrasts clear.
Why it matters today

Stolen idols are returning: Nataraja and other bronzes are repatriated by US and UK museums. The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972 governs trade. Chola bronzes are among India’s GI-protected craft (Swamimalai bronze icons). Nataraja is the logo of the Indian government’s cultural bodies.
How to answer

“Compare the Gandhara and Mathura schools.” Use a table: patron, material, influence, features. “Chola bronzes represent the height of Indian metal sculpture.” Prelims tip: Gandhara = grey schist, Hellenistic; Mathura = red sandstone, indigenous; Amaravati = white marble; lost-wax = Chola and Harappan.
Painting: Ajanta to the Miniature Schools
Colour and story on walls and paper
Painting questions in Prelims ask for school, region and theme. In Mains they ask about Mughal and Rajput contrast or Company paintings.
Prehistoric and early

Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh), rock paintings of the Stone Age, a UNESCO site (2003). Ajanta (Maharashtra), 2nd century BCE to c. 480 CE: Buddhist cave murals. Fresco secco technique. Themes: Jataka tales, Padmapani and Vajrapani, the Mother and Child panel. Bagh caves (Madhya Pradesh). Sittanavasal (Jain, Tamil Nadu). Ellora has few paintings.
Pala, Jain and Pre-Mughal

Pala (Buddhist palm-leaf manuscripts of Nalanda, Vikramashila). Jain western Indian manuscripts (Kalpasutra, Gujarat), with bold lines and large eyes, often silver and gold ink. Sultanate : Persian influence, e.g. Nimatnama. Vijayanagara : Lepakshi murals.
Mughal painting

Rooted in Persian miniature. Humayun brought Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd as-Samad. Akbar : Hamzanama ; Razmnama ; Daswanth, Basawan. Jahangir : naturalism, portraits, birds and flowers; Ustad Mansur (falcons, flowers); Bishandas. Shah Jahan : refined, formal. Aurangzeb : court patronage fell; artists left for provincial courts. Features: realism, perspective, portraits, durbar scenes, borders.
Rajasthani and Pahari schools

Rajasthani (Mewar, Bundi, Kishangarh, Jaipur, Marwar): bold colours, Ragamala, Krishna Lila, Gita Govinda. Kishangarh: Bani Thani (Nihal Chand), long eyes and slender faces. Pahari (Basohli, Guler, Kangra): soft colours, lyrical, Radha-Krishna; Kangra painting under Raja Sansar Chand, 18th century; Nainsukh of Guler. Basohli: bold and early (17th century).
Deccan, Company and modern

Deccani : Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmednagar; rich colours, Ragamala. Company school (late 18th century): Indian artists for British patrons, with natural history subjects; Patna Kalam. Raja Ravi Varma : oleo-prints, Hindu gods in realistic European style. Bengal School (Abanindranath Tagore, Bharat Mata ); Nandalal Bose (Constitution illustrations); Amrita Sher-Gil; Progressive Artists’ Group, 1947 (Souza, Husain, Raza).
Folk paintings

Madhubani (Bihar, GI), Warli (Maharashtra, geometric on mud walls), Pattachitra (Odisha, West Bengal), Kalamkari (Andhra, pen work), Tanjore, Phad (Rajasthan scroll), Gond, Kalighat, Pithora, Cheriyal scrolls. Many have GI tags. Padma awards often go to these artists (e.g. Jivya Soma Mashe, Warli).
Who gets credit: patron or painter?

Court painting names painters rarely; the studio, karkhana , worked under a patron. Mughal paintings carried the emperor’s taste. The Bengal School turned to Asian spiritual tradition as an anti-colonial act, while Ravi Varma’s mass prints shaped popular religion. Debate: nationalism versus realism.
Why it matters today

Madhubani on railway stations and the Warli wall art on public buildings link craft to livelihood schemes. GI tags protect makers. The National Gallery of Modern Art (Delhi, 1954) and National Museum hold masterpieces. The “One District One Product” scheme promotes such crafts.
How to answer

“Mughal and Rajput painting: similarities and differences.” “Ajanta paintings in the history of Indian art.” Prelims tip: Bani Thani = Kishangarh; Hamzanama = Akbar; Kangra = Pahari; Patna Kalam = Company school; Bhimbetka = prehistoric; Ajanta = fresco secco, Buddhist.
Classical and Folk Dances
Dance is a favourite Prelims topic
Questions ask which dance belongs to which state, who the exponents are, and what is classical. The Natya Shastra and the Sangeet Natak Akademi are the key reference points.
What makes a dance classical

The Natya Shastra of Bharata (c. 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE) gives the base: nritta (pure dance), nritya (expressive dance), natya (drama); abhinaya (expression) and rasa (mood). The Sangeet Natak Akademi (1953) recognises eight classical forms; the Ministry of Culture (2000) added Chhau in debate but does not list it. The commonly listed eight: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Kathakali, Sattriya, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam.
Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi

Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu): from Sadir of temple devadasis ; Tanjore Quartet (Chinnaiah, Ponniah, Sivanandam, Vadivelu). Alarippu , jatiswaram , varnam , tillana . Revived by E. Krishna Iyer and Rukmini Devi Arundale (Kalakshetra, 1936). Cut off the “devadasi” tag. Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh): Siddhendra Yogi; originally male Brahmin troupes; tarangam (dance on a brass plate).
Kathak and Odissi

Kathak (north India): kathakars (storytellers); Persian influence under the Mughals; gharanas Jaipur, Lucknow, Banaras; tatkar , chakkars ; Birju Maharaj, Sitara Devi. Odissi (Odisha): temple maharis , Khandagiri-Udayagiri carvings; tribhanga posture; Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda ; Kelucharan Mohapatra.
Kathakali, Mohiniyattam, Sattriya, Manipuri

Kathakali (Kerala): elaborate make-up and costume; stories from the epics; mudras ; Vallathol revived it (Kerala Kalamandalam, 1930). Mohiniyattam (Kerala): female solo; lasya style; swaying movements. Sattriya (Assam): Sankardeva (15th century), monasteries ( sattras ); recognised in 2000. Manipuri : Vaishnava Raslila; soft, lyrical; costume kumil ; Ras Leela, Pung cholom.
Folk and tribal dance

Garba, Dandiya (Gujarat); Bhangra, Giddha (Punjab); Lavani, Koli (Maharashtra); Ghoomar, Kalbelia (Rajasthan, Kalbelia in UNESCO ICH list 2010). Bihu (Assam); Chhau (Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal; UNESCO 2010); Yakshagana (Karnataka); Theyyam (Kerala); Dollu Kunitha; Karakattam; Garadi; Nati (Himachal). Tribal: Ho, Santhal, Gond, Naga dances.
Institutions and honours

Sangeet Natak Akademi (1952 inaugurated, 1953 constituted), National School of Drama, Kalakshetra, Kerala Kalamandalam, Sangeet Natak Akademi Awards, Padma awards. UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Kutiyattam (2008), Chhau (2010), Kalbelia (2010), Garba of Gujarat (inscribed December 2023).
Tradition or classicisation?

Historians such as Avanthi Meduri and Janet O’Shea examine how the 20th-century nationalist revival “classicised” Sadir by removing devadasis from the stage and promoting a respectable Brahmanical image. Critics say this erased hereditary women artists. Others credit Rukmini Devi with saving the art.
Why it matters today

Dance is soft power: ICCR and Indian missions send troupes abroad. Garba’s UNESCO listing, Yoga Day and Padma awards to folk artists show state support. Livelihood concerns of folk artists and the ban on dancing in public have been debated; Sangeet Natak Akademi offers pensions to senior artists.
How to answer

“Classical dances of India reflect the diversity of regional culture. Discuss.” “Differences between Bharatanatyam and Kathak.” Prelims tip: Sattriya = Assam, Sankardeva; Kuchipudi = Andhra; Mohiniyattam = Kerala female; Odissi = Odisha, tribhanga; Chhau and Kalbelia = UNESCO lists.
Music and Theatre Traditions
Sound and stage
The split between Hindustani and Carnatic music, the gharanas and the lineage of folk theatre are staples of Prelims. Mains asks for cultural synthesis.
Roots and two streams

The Natya Shastra and later Sangita Ratnakara (Sharngadeva, 13th century) are textual roots. Music divides into Hindustani (north) and Carnatic (south) after the 13th to 14th century, with Persian influence in the north. Key concepts: raga (melodic frame), tala (rhythm), swara (note), shruti (microtone).
Hindustani music

Dhrupad : old, solemn; Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior; Tansen at Akbar’s court; Swami Haridas. Khayal : Amir Khusrau credited (disputed); Sultan Husain Sharqi; grew under Sadarang in Mohammad Shah’s time. Thumri, Tappa, Dadra, Ghazal : light forms. Gharanas : Gwalior, Agra, Kirana, Jaipur-Atrauli, Patiala, Rampur-Sahaswan. Instruments: sitar, sarod, santoor, tabla, shehnai. Ravi Shankar, Ali Akbar Khan, Bismillah Khan, Bhimsen Joshi.
Carnatic music

Foundation: Purandara Dasa (father of Carnatic music). The Trinity : Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, Shyama Shastri (18th century, Thanjavur). Forms: kriti , varnam , tillana , ragam-tanam-pallavi . Instruments: veena, mridangam, violin, ghatam, nadaswaram. M. S. Subbulakshmi (Bharat Ratna 1998), M. Balamuralikrishna. Melakarta system of 72 parent ragas (Venkatamakhin, 17th century; later reworked).
Other musical streams

Folk: Baul (Bengal), Bhatiyali , Pandavani (Chhattisgarh), Lavani , Alha . Devotional: Rabindra Sangeet, Qawwali (Sufi; Amir Khusrau), Abhangs (Maharashtra), Sufi kalam. Modern: film music and fusion. Bands and the Vande Mataram and Jana Gana Mana traditions run through all of them.
Sanskrit and classical theatre

Sanskrit drama: Bhasa, Kalidasa ( Abhijnana Shakuntalam ), Shudraka ( Mrichchhakatika ), Bhavabhuti, Vishakhadatta ( Mudrarakshasa ). Kutiyattam (Kerala), the only surviving Sanskrit theatre tradition, is a UNESCO Masterpiece (2001, listed ICH 2008). Performed by Chakyars and Nambiars .
Folk and modern theatre

Folk : Ramlila, Raslila, Nautanki (UP), Jatra (Bengal), Tamasha (Maharashtra), Bhavai (Gujarat), Yakshagana, Therukoothu, Pandavani, Bhand Pather (Kashmir), Ankia Naat (Assam). Modern : Parsi theatre; IPTA (1943); Habib Tanvir (Naya Theatre, Charandas Chor ); Utpal Dutt; Girish Karnad; Vijay Tendulkar ( Ghashiram Kotwal ); National School of Drama (1959, Ebrahim Alkazi).
Folk versus classical

Many treat folk and classical as high-low. Others see them as a loop: classical forms draw on folk tunes, folk forms borrow classical technique. The gharana system faces a debate on whether it is a closed lineage or an open school. The impact of recording and film on oral tradition also divides historians.
Why it matters today

Bismillah Khan, Ravi Shankar and Zakir Hussain made Indian music global. Tansen Samaroh (Gwalior), Sawai Gandharva festival and the Thyagaraja Aradhana keep tradition alive. Copyright in folk songs, GI claims and the Gurukul vs digital learning debate continue. Sangeet Natak Akademi and the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya preserve the arts.
How to answer

“Compare Hindustani and Carnatic music.” “Folk theatre as a medium of social change.” Prelims tip: Trinity = Tyagaraja, Dikshitar, Shyama Shastri; Purandara Dasa = father of Carnatic; dhrupad = Man Singh Tomar; Kutiyattam = Kerala, UNESCO.
Indian Literature and Schools of Philosophy
The ideas behind the art
UPSC asks about Vedic texts, Buddhist canon, Sangam works, and the six schools of philosophy. This is high-yield theory with simple pairings.
Vedic and Sanskrit literature

Vedas : Rig, Sama, Yajur, Atharva; Brahmanas , Aranyakas , Upanishads (Vedanta). Epics : Ramayana (Valmiki), Mahabharata (Vyasa; Bhagavad Gita in the Bhishma Parva). Puranas . Classical : Kalidasa ( Meghaduta , Raghuvamsha ), Banabhatta ( Harshacharita ), Kalhana ( Rajatarangini , c. 1148, Kashmir), Panini ( Ashtadhyayi ), Kautilya ( Arthashastra ), Bharata (Natya Shastra).
Pali, Prakrit and Tamil

Buddhist : Tripitaka (Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma) in Pali; Jataka ; Dipavamsa , Mahavamsa (Sri Lanka). Jain : Agamas in Ardha-Magadhi. Sangam (Tamil): Tolkappiyam , Ettuthokai , Pattuppattu ; epics Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal) and Manimekalai (Sattanar); Tirukkural (Tiruvalluvar).
Medieval and regional

Tamil Bhakti hymns: Tevaram , Nalayira Divya Prabandham . Kannada: Pampa. Marathi: Dnyaneshwar’s Dnyaneshwari . Bengali: Chandidas, Chaitanya Charitamrita . Hindi: Kabir, Tulsidas ( Ramcharitmanas ), Surdas, Malik Muhammad Jayasi ( Padmavat ). Persian: Amir Khusrau, Abul Fazl ( Akbarnama , Ain-i-Akbari ), Babur’s Baburnama . Urdu: Mir, Ghalib.
Modern literature

Bankim Chandra ( Anandamath , 1882; Vande Mataram ), Tagore ( Gitanjali ; Nobel 1913), Premchand, Subramania Bharati, Mahadevi Varma, Sarat Chandra. Jnanpith Award (since 1965; first to G. Sankara Kurup). Sahitya Akademi Award (1954). The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages; classical language status given to Tamil (2004), Sanskrit (2005), Telugu and Kannada (2008), Malayalam (2013), Odia (2014), and Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali (October 2024).
Orthodox schools (astika)

Accept the Vedas. Six darshanas : Nyaya (Gautama, logic), Vaisheshika (Kanada, atomism), Sankhya (Kapila, dualism of purusha and prakriti ), Yoga (Patanjali, Yoga Sutras ), Mimamsa (Jaimini, ritual), Vedanta (Badarayana; Shankara’s Advaita, Ramanuja’s Vishishtadvaita, Madhva’s Dvaita).
Heterodox schools (nastika)

Buddhism : Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, anatta ; schools Theravada, Mahayana (Nagarjuna, Madhyamika; Asanga, Yogachara), Vajrayana. Jainism : Mahavira, 24 Tirthankaras, anekantavada , syadvada , five vows; Svetambara and Digambara. Charvaka (Lokayata): materialism; only perception is knowledge. Ajivika : fatalism, Makkhali Gosala.
Was Indian philosophy only religion?

Scholars like Debiprasad Chattopadhyaya ( Lokayata , 1959) stress the materialist strand. Amartya Sen in The Argumentative Indian (2005) shows a long tradition of public debate and dissent. Orientalists tended to present India as only mystical; recent writers show logic, science and politics (Arthashastra) as equally old.
Why it matters today

Classical language status brings funds for chairs and centres: in October 2024 five more languages were added, making 11. Yoga was inscribed by UNESCO in 2016 (ICH). Ideas of ahimsa and anekanta shaped Gandhi and today’s ideas of pluralism. The Constitution’s Eighth Schedule and Article 351 on Hindi tie to this literary heritage.
How to answer

“Discuss the contribution of the six schools of Indian philosophy.” “Indian philosophy is more than religion. Comment.” Prelims tip: Rajatarangini = Kalhana; Silappadikaram = Ilango Adigal; Sankhya = Kapila; Vaisheshika = Kanada; Advaita = Shankara; anekantavada = Jainism; first Jnanpith = Sankara Kurup (1965).
Heritage, UNESCO Sites and Cultural Policy
Current affairs meets static GK
Each year India adds sites; UPSC asks about them. Know the categories, the lists and the institutions.
UNESCO lists

World Heritage Convention (1972; India ratified 1977): cultural, natural and mixed sites. India has 44 World Heritage Sites as of July 2025 (36 cultural, 7 natural, 1 mixed). The Intangible Cultural Heritage convention (2003; India ratified 2005) gives a representative list. India’s ICH elements include Kutiyattam, Vedic chanting, Ramlila, Ramman, Chhau, Kalbelia, Mudiyettu, Sankirtana of Manipur, Yoga (2016), Kumbh Mela (2017), Durga Puja in Kolkata (2021) and Garba (2023).
Recent inscriptions

2021: Dholavira, Ramappa temple (Telangana). 2023: Santiniketan (West Bengal) and Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas. 2024: Moidams (Charaideo, Assam; Ahom burial mounds), India’s 43rd. 2025: Maratha Military Landscapes (12 forts, July 2025), India’s 44th. Tentative list contains many more; India also hosted the 46th World Heritage Committee in New Delhi (July 2024).
Memory of the World and other lists

The Memory of the World Register lists documentary heritage. India’s entries include the Rig Veda manuscripts (2007) and, in 2025, manuscripts of the Bhagavad Gita and the Natyashastra. Check the latest list before the exam. UNESCO Creative Cities Network : Jaipur (crafts), Varanasi (music), Chennai (music), Srinagar (crafts), Kozhikode (literature, 2023) and Gwalior (music, 2023).
Institutions

ASI (1861, Alexander Cunningham): protects monuments under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 ; prohibited area 100 m, regulated area 200 m (2010 amendment). Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972 . INTACH (1984), National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities , Adopt a Heritage (2017, “Apni Dharohar, Apni Pehchaan”). Ministry of Culture: Sangeet Natak Akademi, Sahitya Akademi, Lalit Kala Akademi (all 1950s), National Museum, ICCR.
Constitution and policy

Article 29 (right to conserve culture), Article 49 (DPSP: protect monuments), Article 51A(f) (duty to value the composite culture), and Entry 67 of Union List (ancient monuments of national importance), Entry 12 of State List. The Heritage cities scheme HRIDAY (2015) and PRASAD (pilgrimage), Swadesh Darshan and the Central Vista are policy tools. Heritage by law includes folk and intangible forms through the Guru-Shishya scheme.
Conservation versus development

Tourism pressures at Taj Mahal, Hampi and Khajuraho; encroachments; commercial use of monuments for events; restoration versus preservation (Ayodhya and Konark restoration choices). The Supreme Court’s Taj Trapezium orders and Vishnu Bhagwan’s case show tension. Some argue for community-led conservation and local jobs.
Why it matters today

Repatriation of antiquities (hundreds of objects returned in the last decade), the Bodhgaya and Ajanta tourism circuits and the push for new inscriptions show heritage as soft power. Debates about renaming and the Places of Worship Act 1991 show the legal side.
How to answer

“What steps has India taken to protect its cultural heritage?” “Mention World Heritage Sites inscribed recently and the criteria.” Prelims tip: Know the latest inscriptions and the difference between WHS (tangible) and ICH (intangible). Always check the current number from UNESCO or the Ministry of Culture.
European Companies and the Battle of Plassey
A trading company became a state

Trade, not conquest, brought Europeans to India. Within about 150 years of Vasco da Gama landing at Calicut (1498), one company held the richest province of India. Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764) are the hinge of modern Indian history. UPSC asks two things again and again: why the English won over other Europeans, and how a trading firm became a ruler.
The order of arrival

Portuguese : Vasco da Gama, 1498. Albuquerque took Goa in 1510. Their cartaz (naval pass) system controlled sea trade. Dutch : United East India Company, 1602. Centred on the spice islands of Indonesia, with posts such as Pulicat. English : East India Company chartered 31 December 1600. First factory at Surat, 1613. Danes : 1616; Serampore and Tranquebar. French : Compagnie des Indes, 1664 under Colbert. Pondicherry, founded 1674.
Why the English won

Historians offer several reasons. Sea power : the Royal Navy was stronger than the French fleet. Finance : a stable parliamentary government, a strong bank system and company shareholders who wanted dividends. Base : Bengal, Bombay and Madras were rich and could fund wars, while Pondicherry could not. Leaders : Clive and Eyre Coote against a faction-ridden French command. Industrial change and a trained army also helped later. The French were also distracted by wars in Europe and had less state backing than expected.
The Carnatic Wars

Three wars were fought on the Coromandel coast between the English and French (1746 to 1763), tied to the Austrian Succession and Seven Years’ wars in Europe. The first showed that a small, disciplined European-drilled force could beat large Indian armies (the battle of St Thome, 1746). Dupleix backed rival claimants in Hyderabad and the Carnatic. Clive’s seizure of Arcot (1751) turned the tide. The third war ended with the French defeat at Wandiwash (1760, Eyre Coote). The Treaty of Paris (1763) left Pondicherry to the French as a trading post only.
Plassey, 23 June 1757

Siraj-ud-daulah became Nawab of Bengal in 1756. He seized Calcutta (the “Black Hole” story is doubted by many historians). Clive retook it and then plotted with the nawab’s own commanders. At Plassey, Mir Jafar , the commander, held back his troops. Others in the plot included Rai Durlabh, Yar Lutuf Khan, the banker Jagat Seth and Omichand. The battle was little more than a skirmish, yet it gave the Company the throne of Bengal in all but name. Mir Jafar became nawab and paid huge sums.
Buxar and the Diwani

Mir Qasim, Mir Jafar’s son-in-law, tried to rule independently and abolished internal duties. He joined Shuja-ud-daula of Awadh and Shah Alam II, the Mughal emperor. They were beaten at Buxar, 1764 (Hector Munro). By the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) Clive got the Diwani (revenue rights) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa from Shah Alam II. The Nawab kept the nizamat (policing and justice). This was the dual government (1765 to 1772), power without responsibility, which Warren Hastings ended.
Was Plassey a battle or a conspiracy?

Nationalist historians such as Bipan Chandra stress that Plassey was won by treachery and by Bengal’s own elite, not by arms. Buxar was the real military test. Yet Plassey mattered because it handed the Company Bengal’s wealth. This funded armies and bought Indian-made goods with Indian revenue, a point Dadabhai Naoroji later used in his drain theory. Some historians, such as C. A. Bayly, say the Company’s rise also depended on Indian bankers and local elites who chose to back it.
Why it matters today

Bengal’s early colonisation shaped Calcutta’s rise as capital (till 1911) and the Permanent Settlement later. The memory of dependence on foreign trading power is behind India’s caution about economic dependence and strategic autonomy. Goa remained Portuguese until 1961, and Pondicherry stayed French until its de facto transfer in 1954. These are the last pieces of European empire in India.
How to answer

Mains: “Why did the English East India Company succeed against other European powers in India?” Structure: sea power, finance, base in Bengal, leadership, disunity of Indian rulers. Mains: “Assess the importance of Plassey and Buxar.” Plassey gave political control; Buxar gave legal and military legitimacy via the Diwani. Prelims tip: remember the order of company founding (Portuguese 1498, English 1600, Dutch 1602, Danes 1616, French 1664) and who held the Diwani (Clive, 1765).
Expansion of British Power to 1857
From Bengal to the whole subcontinent
Between 1757 and 1856 the Company grew from a Bengal ruler to the paramount power. UPSC likes the methods of expansion and the policy of each Governor-General. A clean timeline wins marks.
Three ways of expansion

War and conquest : Mysore, the Marathas, Sindh, the Punjab. Diplomacy and the Subsidiary Alliance : Wellesley. Annexation by policy : the Doctrine of Lapse and “misgovernment” (Awadh). The Company also used the policy of the ring fence (Warren Hastings) and subordinate isolation (Lord Hastings, 1813 to 1823), and later subordinate union (Dalhousie).
Mysore Wars

Haidar Ali and then Tipu Sultan modernised the army and used rockets. Four wars were fought. First (1767 to 69): Treaty of Madras. Second (1780 to 84): Treaty of Mangalore. Third (1790 to 92): Cornwallis; Treaty of Seringapatam; Tipu lost half his territory. Fourth (1799): Wellesley; Tipu died defending Seringapatam. The Wodeyars were restored in Mysore under a subsidiary alliance.
Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley, 1798 to 1805)

The ruler accepted a British force, paid for it, expelled other Europeans and agreed not to deal with other states without the Company’s consent. A British Resident lived in his court. First to sign: Hyderabad (1798). Then Mysore, Tanjore, Awadh, the Peshwa (Treaty of Bassein, 1802), Bhonsle and Scindia. Rulers lost sovereignty. The Company gained a large army paid by others.
Marathas and the Punjab

Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) under Lord Hastings ended the Peshwa’s rule; Bajirao II was pensioned at Bithur. The Marathas had been weakened by internal quarrels. Sindh was taken in 1843 (Charles Napier). In the Punjab , Ranjit Singh signed the Treaty of Amritsar (1809) with the English. After his death (1839) came two Sikh wars (1845 to 46; 1848 to 49). Dalhousie annexed the Punjab in 1849.
Doctrine of Lapse

Lord Dalhousie (1848 to 1856) held that when a dependent ruler died without a natural heir, the state passed to the Company. Adopted sons were not recognised. States annexed: Satara (1848), Jaitpur and Sambalpur, Baghat, Udaipur, Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854). Awadh was annexed in 1856 on grounds of misrule. Dalhousie also built railways and the telegraph. The Nana Sahib and the Rani of Jhansi lost pensions and claims, which fed the Revolt of 1857.
Conquest by accident or design?

The older English view, from John Seeley, says the empire was acquired “in a fit of absence of mind”. Nationalist and Marxist historians stress deliberate aggression driven by revenue needs and the army’s costs. Many modern historians point to a “fiscal-military” state that needed ever more revenue to pay its own army.
Why it matters today

The legacy of princely states and the Residents’ system shaped the 1947 integration problem. Border questions with Burma, Nepal and Afghanistan began in the same period (Treaty of Sugauli 1816 with Nepal). Tipu and the Rani of Jhansi remain symbols in public memory and in school texts.
How to answer

“Discuss the policy of Subsidiary Alliance and its effects.” Give terms, signatories, effect on rulers and the Company. “The Doctrine of Lapse was a cause of 1857.” Give the states annexed and who lost. Prelims tip: match the policy to the person, and the treaty to the war (Bassein 1802, Seringapatam 1792, Mangalore 1784).
Land Revenue Systems and the Drain of Wealth
The economic engine of empire

Land revenue was the largest source of Company income. How it was fixed changed rural India and caused famines and debt. Naoroji and R. C. Dutt then showed how wealth left India. Few topics are asked as often.
Three land revenue systems

Permanent Settlement (Zamindari) , 1793, Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, Varanasi: Cornwallis. Ryotwari , 1820 (Thomas Munro, Madras), also Bombay: the cultivator is the owner. Mahalwari , 1822 (Holt Mackenzie), 1833 (Bird): the village community pays together. North-West Provinces, Punjab. About 19% of area was zamindari, 51% ryotwari and 30% mahalwari under British India.
Permanent Settlement, 1793

The Company fixed the revenue permanently. Zamindars became owners and paid a fixed sum, about 10/11 of the rent collected. Failure meant the land was auctioned (the Sunset Law). Effects: Company revenue became certain. Zamindars gained but many fell out and absentee landlords grew. Peasants had no protection of tenure until the Bengal Tenancy Act (1885). The land became a commodity and moneylending rose. Cornwallis hoped for improvement; little came.
Ryotwari and Mahalwari

Ryotwari : settlement directly with each cultivator, revised every 20 to 30 years. Rates were often high, around half the produce, which forced peasants into debt. Seen as “fairer” but in practice heavy. Mahalwari : the village ( mahal ) headmen collected revenue. Revision every 30 years. In all systems revenue was fixed in cash and in advance, whatever the harvest.
Commercialisation and de-industrialisation

Cash demand pushed farmers to grow cotton, indigo, jute, opium and sugarcane. This is commercialisation of agriculture , driven by the market and often by the colonial state, not farmer prosperity. The Deccan Riots (1875) and the Indigo Revolt (1859 to 60) followed. De-industrialisation: cheap Lancashire cloth and heavy duties on Indian goods (and free trade after 1813 and 1833) ruined handicrafts. Weavers moved to farming, raising pressure on land.
The drain of wealth

Dadabhai Naoroji , Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901): drain was a “material and moral” loss. R. C. Dutt , Economic History of India (1901 to 03). Home Charges : pensions, interest, salaries and army costs paid in London. The drain meant exports for which India got no imports in return. Naoroji put it at about £30 million a year (an estimate, disputed).
How much did the drain cost?

Nationalists such as Naoroji, Dutt, M. G. Ranade and R. P. Dutt saw impoverishment. Some economists, such as Morris D. Morris, argued that India was not that damaged and that railways and irrigation helped. Utsa Patnaik has recently estimated very large figures, which others dispute. The debate is about method, not that Home Charges existed.
Why it matters today

Zamindari abolition was the first big land reform after 1947 (First Amendment and Ninth Schedule, 1951). Tenancy and land ceilings, and rural debt, still trace back to these systems. The drain argument shaped India’s early planning and its self-reliance stance. Famine memory shaped food security laws.
How to answer

“Examine the impact of British land revenue policy on Indian agriculture.” Structure: three systems, features, effects on peasants, commercialisation, famines. “Explain the drain of wealth theory.” Define, give Naoroji and Dutt, Home Charges, evidence, criticism. Prelims tip: Permanent Settlement areas, Munro and Ryotwari, and the year of each.
Education, Press and Administrative Changes
The colonial state-building story
British rule built institutions that still run India: civil services, courts, police, schools, a free-ish press. It did so to serve empire. UPSC asks you to weigh both sides.
Administrative pillars

Lord Cornwallis, “father of the civil services”, separated revenue and justice, raised pay and created a covenanted service. The steel frame was the ICS. Police: district superintendent system (Cornwallis), Police Act 1861. Army: mostly Indian sepoys with British officers; recruitment later shifted to the “martial races” after 1857. Judiciary: Cornwallis Code (1793), the codification of laws by Macaulay (Law Commission 1833), High Courts Act 1861.
Civil services

Entry by exam in London from 1855 (Indian Civil Service). Satyendranath Tagore was the first Indian in 1863. Age limit was cut to 19 in 1878 to keep Indians out. Indianisation was demanded by the Congress from 1885; simultaneous exams in India began only in 1922. The Lee Commission (1923 to 24) recommended direct recruitment, with 40% Europeans, 40% Indians direct and 20% promoted.
Education policy

Charter Act 1813 : Rs 1 lakh yearly for education. Orientalist–Anglicist debate : Macaulay’s Minute (1835) backed English; Bentinck accepted it. Wood’s Despatch (1854) : “Magna Carta of English education”; universities at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857); departments of education; grants-in-aid; vernacular primary schools. Hunter Commission (1882) : primary and secondary education. Sadler Commission (1917 to 19) : universities. Hartog Committee (1929) : primary education.
The “downward filtration” idea

Macaulay wanted an English-educated class to “filter” knowledge down to the masses. It never worked. Literacy was about 12% in 1947. Female and rural education lagged. Yet the English-educated class gave rise to the nationalist leadership and to reformers. Colleges also taught ideas of liberty and nation that were turned against the Raj.
The Press

1780: Hickey’s Bengal Gazette , India’s first newspaper. Censorship Act 1799 (Wellesley). Metcalfe freed the press in 1835 (the “liberator of the press”). Licensing Act 1857. Vernacular Press Act 1878 (Lytton) — repealed 1882 by Ripon. Newspaper (Incitement to Offences) Act 1908; Indian Press Act 1910. Tilak’s Kesari and Mahratta , Amrita Bazar Patrika , The Hindu and Bombay Chronicle were nationalist voices.
Law and policing

Regulating Act of 1773 set up the Supreme Court at Calcutta. Equal law was claimed, but there were separate courts for Europeans (the Ilbert Bill row of 1883, which gave Indian judges power over Europeans, was withdrawn in a diluted form). Sedition (S.124A) was added in 1870. The Arms Act 1878 disarmed Indians. Laws were written to protect the empire.
Gift or tool?

Colonial writers say that Britain gave India modern institutions. Nationalists such as Bipan Chandra reply that institutions were built to maintain the empire, and education was a means to produce clerks. Sumit Sarkar and others stress that Indians used these tools in their own ways. A balanced answer says: unintended gains, intended control.
Why it matters today

The All India Services, the IPC (now replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, in force 1 July 2024), the district collector and the police structure all trace back here. The sedition law is in debate; the Supreme Court in 2022 put S.124A on hold. The three-language question and English medium still run on the Macaulay legacy.
How to answer

“Macaulay’s Minute of 1835 and its impact.” “The Indian Civil Service was the steel frame of the empire. Discuss.” “Trace the growth of the press under the British.” Prelims tip: Wood’s Despatch 1854, Hunter 1882, Sadler 1917, Hartog 1929; Vernacular Press Act 1878 by Lytton, repealed by Ripon.
The Revolt of 1857: Causes, Course, Consequences
The first big challenge to Company rule
1857 is the single most examined event in modern India. Know its causes in layers, who led where, and what changed afterwards. The name itself is a debate.
Causes in layers

Political : Doctrine of Lapse, annexation of Awadh, pension stops for Nana Sahib, insult to the Mughal emperor. Economic : land revenue, loss of jobs for artisans, taluqdars dispossessed in Awadh. Social and religious : fear of conversion; laws on widow remarriage and the Religious Disabilities Act 1850. Military : low pay, the General Service Enlistment Act 1856 (overseas service), caste insults, discrimination. Immediate : the Enfield rifle cartridge, said to be greased with cow and pig fat.
The outbreak

Mangal Pandey of the 34th Native Infantry was hanged at Barrackpore in March 1857. On 10 May 1857 sepoys at Meerut rose, freed their comrades and marched to Delhi. They proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar as emperor. Soon Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Bihar (Arrah) and parts of central India joined. The Bengal army was the core. The Madras and Bombay armies and the Sikhs and Gurkhas largely stayed loyal.
Leaders and centres

Delhi : Bahadur Shah, Bakht Khan. Kanpur : Nana Sahib, with Tantia Tope. Lucknow : Begum Hazrat Mahal. Jhansi : Rani Lakshmibai. Arrah (Bihar) : Kunwar Singh. Faizabad : Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah. Bareilly : Khan Bahadur Khan. British commanders included John Nicholson, Henry Havelock, Colin Campbell, Hugh Rose.
Suppression

Delhi fell on 20 September 1857. Havelock and Campbell relieved Lucknow in November. Jhansi fell in April 1858 and Rani Lakshmibai died at Gwalior in June 1858. Tantia Tope was captured and executed in 1859. Bahadur Shah was exiled to Rangoon. Failures: no unified plan, no central leader, limited area (not the south or most of the east, nor Punjab), and unequal weapons. Many rulers and big landlords sided with the British.
Mutiny, war of independence, or revolt?

British writers (Lawrence, Kaye) called it a sepoy mutiny . V. D. Savarkar called it the First War of Independence . R. C. Majumdar said it was neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence. S. B. Chaudhuri saw a civil rebellion. Marxists such as Rajni Palme Dutt saw a peasants’ rising. Eric Stokes and Ranajit Guha studied the peasant side. Bipan Chandra calls it a “massive revolt” but without a modern national idea.
Consequences

Government of India Act 1858 : the Crown took over; Secretary of State and a Council in London; Viceroy; Queen’s Proclamation, 1 November 1858. The Company’s Army reorganised: more British soldiers, artillery with Europeans. “Divide and rule” sharpened. Policy of friendship with princes: no more annexations. Interest in social reform dropped.
Why it matters today

Memorials in Delhi, Jhansi, Lucknow and Kanpur and stamps show the revolt’s place in the national story. 2007–08 saw a 150th anniversary debate on the name. The Queen’s Proclamation promised equal treatment, a promise often used by early nationalists.
How to answer

“The Revolt of 1857 was not a sepoy mutiny but a popular rising. Comment.” “Why did it fail?” “Assess its consequences.” Prelims tip: match the leader with the centre; remember the Act of 1858 and the Proclamation; Meerut 10 May 1857.
Reform Movements of the 19th Century
Reform before freedom
Before political nationalism there was a social awakening. UPSC loves matching reformers, organisations, books and years, and asking about their method and limits.
Two currents

Reformist movements used reason and law to fight sati, child marriage and caste. Revivalist ones went back to the past (the Arya Samaj’s “Back to the Vedas”). Both worked in the shadow of colonial rule, missionaries and English education. Hindu, Muslim, Parsi, Sikh and Christian reformers all took part.
Raja Ram Mohan Roy and the Brahmo Samaj

Founded the Atmiya Sabha (1815) and the Brahmo Samaj (1828). Opposed sati, idolatry and polytheism. Lord Bentinck outlawed sati in 1829 (Regulation XVII). Roy wrote Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin and published Sambad Kaumudi and Mirat-ul-Akhbar . Debendranath Tagore revived the Samaj (Tattvabodhini Sabha, 1839). Keshub Chandra Sen split it in 1866. The Native Marriage Act 1872 followed.
Bengal and Western India

Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar : Widow Remarriage Act 1856; girls’ schools. Derozio and Young Bengal: free thought. Ramakrishna and Vivekananda : Ramakrishna Mission (1897). Vivekananda spoke at Chicago in 1893. Prarthana Samaj (1867, Atmaram Pandurang; Ranade, Bhandarkar). Gopal Hari Deshmukh “Lokahitawadi” and Jotirao Phule (Satyashodhak Samaj, 1873).
Arya Samaj and revivalism

Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj (Bombay, 1875), with Satyarth Prakash as its book. His slogan: “go back to the Vedas”. He opposed idol worship, caste by birth and child marriage, and ran the shuddhi movement. Lala Hansraj started the DAV schools (1886 at Lahore). Theosophical Society: Madame Blavatsky and Colonel Olcott (New York 1875; Adyar 1882); Annie Besant led it and founded the Central Hindu College (1898) and the Home Rule League.
Muslim, Parsi, Sikh reform

Aligarh : Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College (1875). Deoband : Muhammad Qasim Nanotvi (1866) — religious purity, later aligned with Congress. Ahmadiyya (1889), Mirza Ghulam Ahmad; Wahabi , Syed Ahmad Barelvi. Parsi : Rahnumae Mazdayasnan Sabha (1851), Naoroji and Behramji Malabari. Sikh : Singh Sabha (1873); Akali movement, 1920s.
Methods and results

Reformers used journals, schools, petitions and legislation. Achievements: sati ban 1829, widow remarriage 1856, Age of Consent Act 1891 (raised to 12 after Malabari’s campaign), Special Marriage Act 1872, Sarda Act 1929. Limits: mostly urban and upper caste; ignored the lowest castes and peasants; rarely questioned colonial rule. Some reformers’ religious revivalism fed communal identities.
Renaissance or limited awakening?

Historians such as Sumit Sarkar question the word “renaissance”. Others see in these movements a rational base for nationalism, as Bipan Chandra argues. Dalit and feminist scholars say the reformers’ concerns were partial: they looked at women through upper-caste reform, and Phule and Ambedkar had to push further.
Why it matters today

The reform legacy underlies the Constitution’s Articles 14 to 17 and 25 to 28, the Hindu Code Bills (1955 to 56), and the Supreme Court’s 2018 Sabarimala and 2017 triple talaq (Shayara Bano) judgments. Debates on a Uniform Civil Code (Article 44) echo reformers’ questions.
How to answer

“The 19th century reform movements were both reformist and revivalist. Discuss.” “Role of Raja Ram Mohan Roy in modernising India.” Prelims tip: match organisation to founder and year; Brahmo 1828, Prarthana 1867, Arya Samaj 1875, Satyashodhak 1873, Theosophical 1875.
Caste, Tribal and Peasant Movements
Movements from below
Reformers were often upper caste. Alongside them rose movements of the oppressed, tribes and peasants. UPSC asks for names, places, years and the colonial causes.
Why they happened

Colonial land revenue, forest laws, moneylenders and outsiders ( dikus ) hurt peasants and tribes. Missionaries and English education opened new ideas to lower castes. The state’s census (from 1871 to 1881) also hardened caste identity.
Caste movements: the south and west

Jotirao Phule : Gulamgiri (1873); Satyashodhak Samaj; first girls’ school at Pune, 1848 with Savitribai. Self-Respect Movement (1925), E. V. Ramasamy Periyar. SNDP (1903), Sree Narayana Guru, Kerala: “One caste, one religion, one God”. Justice Party (1916) in Madras. Vaikom Satyagraha (1924 to 25) for temple-road entry.
Ambedkar and Gandhi

B. R. Ambedkar : Mahad Satyagraha (1927) for water; burnt the Manusmriti ; Kalaram temple entry (Nashik 1930); Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924); Mooknayak (1920). He argued for separate electorates at the Round Table Conferences. The Poona Pact (1932) with Gandhi gave reserved seats within the general electorate (148 in provincial councils). Gandhi started the Harijan and the All India Harijan Sangh (1932).
Tribal revolts

Santhal Hul (1855 to 56): Sido and Kanhu, Rajmahal hills. Munda Ulgulan (1899 to 1900): Birsa Munda, Chotanagpur. Kol revolt (1831 to 32); Khasi (Tirut Singh, 1829 to 33); Bhil ; Rampa (Alluri Sitarama Raju, 1922 to 24). Chuar, Ho and Kherwar revolts. Causes: loss of land, forest laws (Indian Forest Act 1865, 1878), outsiders and money lenders. Birsa Munda’s movement led to the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908.
Peasant movements before 1900

Indigo Revolt (1859 to 60, Bengal), Digambar and Bishnu Biswas; supported by Neel Darpan (Dinabandhu Mitra); Harish Chandra Mukherjee wrote in the Hindoo Patriot . Pabna agrarian leagues (1873 to 76). Deccan Riots (1875): against moneylenders; Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act 1879. Moplah rebellions, Malabar (1836 to 1921).
Peasant movements after 1900

Champaran (1917), Gandhi’s first satyagraha in India. Kheda (1918) and Bardoli (1928, Sardar Patel). Eka Movement (UP, 1921), Kisan Sabha (Baba Ramchandra; UP Kisan Sabha 1918). All India Kisan Sabha (1936, Lucknow), Swami Sahajanand Saraswati president. Tebhaga (1946 to 47, Bengal) and Telangana (1946 to 51) risings.
Primitive rebels or political actors?

Eric Hobsbawm called such movements “primitive rebellion”. Ranajit Guha and the Subaltern Studies group ( Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency , 1983) argue peasants had their own politics, separate from the elite. Critics say the school underplays Congress mobilisation and class differences among peasants.
Why it matters today

The Fifth and Sixth Schedules, the PESA Act 1996 and the Forest Rights Act 2006 trace tribal anxieties to these revolts. Land reforms, minimum support price and the 2020 farm law protests tie to the peasant past. Birsa Munda’s birth anniversary (15 November) is celebrated as Janjatiya Gaurav Divas since 2021.
How to answer

“Tribal movements in colonial India had different causes from peasant movements. Discuss.” “Compare Phule and Ambedkar on caste.” Prelims tip: leader–place pairs (Birsa–Chotanagpur, Sido-Kanhu–Santhal Parganas) and years of the Poona Pact (1932), All India Kisan Sabha (1936).
Rise of Nationalism and the Moderates
Why India woke up
Nationalism was not given. It grew from economic grievance, a new English-educated middle class, and a shared fight against colonial rule. The Moderates built the base.
Causes of nationalism

Economic exploitation shown by the drain theory. Railways, telegraphs and the post made one market. Western ideas, press and the educated class. Racial arrogance, e.g. the Ilbert Bill (1883) controversy. Lytton’s policies: Vernacular Press Act, Arms Act 1878, the cost of the Afghan war. Earlier associations: British Indian Association (1851), Indian Association (1876, Surendranath Banerjea), Poona Sarvajanik Sabha, Madras Mahajan Sabha (1884).
Founding of the Congress, 1885

A.O. Hume, a retired civil servant, took the lead. The first session met at Bombay (28 December 1885) under W. C. Bonnerjee , with 72 delegates. Dufferin is said to have approved. Radical writers called it the “safety valve” theory; Bipan Chandra rejects it and says Indian leaders used Hume for their own plans. Early presidents: Naoroji (1886, 1893, 1906), Badruddin Tyabji (1887, first Muslim), George Yule (1888, first English).
The Moderates: who and what

Leaders: Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, W. C. Bonnerjee, Surendranath Banerjea, G. K. Gokhale, M. G. Ranade, Romesh Dutt, Madan Mohan Malaviya. Their faith: constitutional agitation, loyalty to the Crown, and the British sense of justice. Methods: prayer, petition, protest. Their demands: expansion of the legislative councils, Indianisation of the ICS and simultaneous exams, cut military costs, protect civil liberties.
Achievements

Built a national platform and political education. Economic critique: Naoroji, Dutt, Ranade, G. V. Joshi. Indian Councils Act 1892 : more members, right to discuss budget, limited indirect election. Pressure on the Welby Commission (1895). The 1893 Congress under Naoroji; 1905 under Gokhale (Servants of India Society founded the same year).
Limits and critique

The Moderates drew support from the educated urban elite only. They had no mass base, believed in the “providential” nature of British rule and won little. The Extremists called their politics “political mendicancy”. Yet Bipan Chandra argues the Moderates did the necessary work: they had to build awareness and a common economic critique first. Lala Lajpat Rai and Tilak later wanted more.
Safety valve or seed of freedom?

The safety valve idea (Lala Lajpat Rai, 1916; later Marxists) says the Congress was started to channel discontent. Anil Seal (Cambridge School) views early nationalism as elite competition for jobs and offices. Bipan Chandra and others see a genuine anti-colonial movement which used moderate means for strategic reasons.
Why it matters today

India’s parliamentary culture, respect for debate and the legal-constitutional style trace to the Moderates. The Servants of India Society idea of public service has echoes in civil society. The Congress, the oldest party, celebrates 28 December as its foundation day.
How to answer

“Evaluate the role of the Moderates in the freedom struggle.” Give methods, demands, achievements, limits. “Causes of the rise of Indian nationalism.” Prelims tip: first Congress president (Bonnerjee), first Muslim (Tyabji, 1887), first woman (Annie Besant 1917; Sarojini Naidu first Indian woman, 1925).
Extremists, Swadeshi and Revolutionaries
From petition to protest
After 1900 a new generation wanted boycott, not begging. The partition of Bengal in 1905 gave them a cause.
Rise of the Extremists

Causes: Moderates’ failure, Curzon’s policies (Calcutta Corporation Act 1899, Official Secrets Act 1904, University Act 1904, partition of Bengal 1905), economic distress (famines, plague), Japan’s victory over Russia in 1905, and the work of Vivekananda and Dayanand. Leaders: Lal-Bal-Pal (Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal) and Aurobindo Ghose.
Partition of Bengal, 1905

Announced July 1905 by Curzon, effective 16 October 1905. East Bengal and Assam (Muslim-majority) separated from West Bengal. The stated reason was administrative efficiency. The real aim was to divide the Hindu and Muslim population and weaken Bengal. 16 October was observed as a day of mourning and rakhi bandhan (Tagore’s songs, e.g. “Amar Sonar Bangla”). The partition was annulled in 1911 at the Delhi Durbar, and the capital moved to Delhi.
Swadeshi and boycott

Declared on 7 August 1905 at the Calcutta Town Hall. Methods: boycott of foreign goods, national education (National Council of Education, 1906; Bengal National College, Aurobindo as principal), samitis (Swadesh Bandhab Samiti, Ashwini Kumar Dutt), swadeshi industry (Bengal Chemicals, Tata Steel, 1907), and the use of melas and festivals (Ganapati, Shivaji). The four aims adopted at the 1906 Calcutta Congress (Naoroji) were Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education.
Surat Split, 1907

At Surat (December 1907) the Congress broke into Moderates and Extremists. The issue: the presidency (Lajpat Rai vs Rash Behari Ghosh) and the resolutions on boycott and swadeshi. The government then repressed the Extremists: Tilak was jailed for six years in Mandalay (1908), Aurobindo and Lajpat Rai were arrested or exiled. The Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 gave separate electorates to Muslims. The two wings reunited at Lucknow, 1916.
Revolutionary nationalism

Bengal : Anushilan Samiti, Jugantar; Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki (1908 Muzaffarpur). Maharashtra : Chapekar brothers (1897, Rand); Savarkar’s Abhinav Bharat. Abroad : India House (Shyamji Krishnavarma, London); Madan Lal Dhingra (1909); Ghadar Party (1913, San Francisco; Lala Har Dayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna); Komagata Maru (1914). The Alipore Bomb case (1908) involved Aurobindo.
Revolutionaries after 1920

After Chauri Chaura the youth turned to the gun. HRA (1924, Sachindranath Sanyal) → Kakori (1925; Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan). HSRA (1928; Bhagat Singh, Chandrashekhar Azad). Saunders’ killing (1928), Assembly bomb (1929), Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev hanged 23 March 1931. Surya Sen’s Chittagong armoury raid (1930). Subhas Bose’s INA is the last wave.
Did violence help?

Gandhi opposed terrorism but admired its courage. Bipan Chandra says revolutionaries gave fearlessness and a symbol but lacked mass support. Their ideas moved towards socialism (HSRA, Bhagat Singh’s “Why I am an atheist”, 1930). Critics point to the narrow and elitist social base.
Why it matters today

Swadeshi lives on in “Make in India” and “Atmanirbhar Bharat”. Dates such as 23 March (Shaheed Diwas) and the memorial at Hussainiwala keep memory alive. The Bengal partition shaped regional identity (1947, 1971).
How to answer

“Differences between the Moderates and Extremists.” Compare goal, methods, social base, leaders. “Significance of the Swadeshi movement.” Prelims tip: 1905 partition, 1906 Muslim League, 1907 Surat, 1909 Morley-Minto, 1911 annulment.
The Gandhian Phase: 1917–1934
The movement becomes mass
Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and turned a movement of the educated into a movement of millions. This is the most tested block of the freedom struggle.
Gandhi’s method

Satyagraha (truth force), ahimsa , non-cooperation, civil disobedience, constructive work (khadi, village industry). He tested it first in Champaran (1917), Ahmedabad mill strike (1918, fast) and Kheda (1918). The Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919) was his first all-India call.
Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh

The Rowlatt Act (March 1919) allowed detention without trial. Hartals followed. On 13 April 1919 General Dyer fired on a crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar; the official toll was 379, Indian estimates over 1,000. Tagore returned his knighthood. The Hunter Committee was appointed. Gandhi called off the movement. The Montagu-Chelmsford reforms (1919) gave dyarchy in provinces.
Non-Cooperation and Khilafat, 1920 to 22

The Khilafat Movement (Ali brothers, Maulana Azad) joined hands. The Congress adopted non-cooperation at Calcutta (special session, Sept 1920) and Nagpur. Boycott of schools, courts, titles and councils; khadi; the Tilak Swaraj Fund. On 5 February 1922 a mob burnt a police station at Chauri Chaura and Gandhi withdrew the movement. Critics were angry. Swarajists (Motilal Nehru and C. R. Das) entered the councils in 1923.
Simon Commission and the Nehru Report

The all-white Simon Commission (1927) led to the cry “Simon Go Back”; Lala Lajpat Rai was injured at Lahore and died in 1928. The Nehru Report (1928) was India’s own constitution plan with dominion status and no separate electorates. Jinnah’s Fourteen Points (1929) answered it. At Lahore (December 1929, Nehru president) the Congress declared Purna Swaraj; 26 January 1930 was marked as Independence Day.
Civil Disobedience Movement, 1930 to 34

Gandhi began the Dandi March on 12 March 1930 with 78 followers from Sabarmati and broke the salt law on 6 April. Mass salt, forest and no-tax actions spread. Peshawar (Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, Khudai Khidmatgars), Sholapur, Dharasana. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931) suspended it. At the Second Round Table Conference (1931) Gandhi was the only Congress delegate. In 1932 the Communal Award (MacDonald) gave separate electorates to the Depressed Classes; Gandhi fasted and signed the Poona Pact . The movement was formally withdrawn in 1934.
Round Table Conferences

First (1930 to 31): Congress absent. Second (September to December 1931): Gandhi attended. Third (1932): Congress absent. They led to the White Paper (1933) and the Government of India Act 1935. Key problem: minority representation. Ambedkar and Jinnah, princes and Liberals (Sapru, Jayakar) took part.
Did Gandhi sell out?

Marxists such as R. P. Dutt and A. R. Desai accuse the Gandhian leadership of stopping movements when peasants and workers turned radical (Chauri Chaura, Gandhi-Irwin pact). Bipan Chandra defends Gandhi: his strategy of struggle, truce and struggle (S-T-S) kept the movement moving and prevented violent repression of weak groups. Subaltern scholars note that peasants gave Gandhi their own meanings.
Why it matters today

Dandi is now a memorial and a symbol of civil disobedience. Satyagraha shaped the Indian way of protest (Right to protest, Article 19). Khadi and the Khadi and Village Industries Commission; the Poona Pact’s reserved seats evolved into SC/ST reservation in legislatures (Articles 330 and 332). 2 October is observed as the International Day of Non-Violence (UN, 2007).
How to answer

“Gandhi transformed the national movement. Elaborate.” “Compare Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience.” “Why was the Poona Pact needed?” Prelims tip: dates of Rowlatt (1919), Chauri Chaura (1922), Dandi (1930), Gandhi-Irwin (1931), Poona Pact (1932).
Towards Freedom: 1935–1947
The endgame
From provincial rule in 1937 to Partition in 1947: this part carries the most dates and the most debate about who is to blame for the split.
1935 and the 1937 elections

The Government of India Act 1935 gave provincial autonomy. In the 1937 elections the Congress won a clear majority in 5 of 11 provinces and formed ministries in 6 provinces in July 1937, later 8 with the NWFP and Assam. The Muslim League did poorly. The refusal to form a coalition in UP deepened distance. Congress ministries resigned in October 1939 over India being dragged into the war.
The war years

1940 Lahore Resolution of the Muslim League (Pakistan). Jinnah’s Two-Nation theory. August Offer 1940 (dominion status after the war, and no veto to minorities); Individual Satyagraha (Vinoba Bhave first). 1942 Cripps Mission : dominion status after the war with the right of provinces to opt out; Gandhi called it a “post-dated cheque”. 8 August 1942: Quit India , “Do or Die”; leaders arrested; underground by Aruna Asaf Ali, Jayaprakash Narayan, Usha Mehta (Congress Radio).
INA and Subhas Bose

Subhas Chandra Bose left India in 1941, reached Germany and in 1943 took over the Indian National Army in Singapore from Rash Behari Bose and Mohan Singh. Provisional Government of Free India (October 1943). Slogans: “Delhi Chalo” and “Jai Hind”. The INA fought in Imphal and Kohima, 1944. After the war the INA trials at the Red Fort (Shah Nawaz, Sehgal, Dhillon) provoked a national outcry (1945 to 46). The Royal Indian Navy Mutiny (February 1946, Bombay) showed that the armed forces were no longer safe.
1945 to 1946: plans and elections

C. R. formula (1944) and Gandhi-Jinnah talks . Wavell Plan and the Simla Conference (June 1945): Jinnah insisted on all Muslim seats. 1946 elections: Congress won most general seats; League won almost all Muslim seats. Cabinet Mission (March to June 1946; Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps, A. V. Alexander): rejected Pakistan, proposed a three-tier federation with groups A, B, C and a Constituent Assembly.
Direct Action to Mountbatten

Jinnah called Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946; riots in Calcutta spread. An Interim Government under Nehru was formed in September 1946; the League joined in October. The Constituent Assembly met on 9 December 1946. On 20 February 1947 Attlee announced that power would be transferred by June 1948. Mountbatten arrived in March 1947, and on 3 June 1947 the Plan for partition was announced. The Indian Independence Act (18 July 1947) created two dominions on 15 August 1947. Radcliffe drew the boundaries.
Who divided India?

Nationalist writers blame the League and the British “divide and rule”. Ayesha Jalal ( The Sole Spokesman , 1985) argues Jinnah used Pakistan as a bargaining chip for equal share at the Centre. Others (Tara Chand, Bipan Chandra) stress communal ideologies since the 1920s. Some stress Congress’s failure to accommodate the League after 1937. Mountbatten’s hurry has been criticised too.
Why it matters today

Radcliffe’s line still decides border disputes and people’s identity. 14 August is observed as Partition Horrors Remembrance Day since 2021. INA ideas shape India’s military memory; 23 January (Bose’s birthday) is Parakram Diwas. The Cripps and Cabinet Mission formulas appear in debates about federalism.
How to answer

“Analyse the Quit India Movement and its significance.” “Why did the Cabinet Mission fail?” “What led to the Partition?” Give long-term (communalism), medium-term (1937, 1940) and short-term causes (1946). Prelims tip: the order of 1940 August Offer, 1942 Cripps, 1945 Wavell, 1946 Cabinet Mission, 1947 Mountbatten.
Women, Dalits and Regions in the Freedom Struggle
A wider lens
The freedom struggle was not only Congress and Gandhi. Recent UPSC questions ask about women, Dalits, tribes and different regions. This lesson gives you the names.
Women in the struggle

Women took part from the Swadeshi days. Gandhi’s call brought thousands into picket lines, salt making and jails. Sarojini Naidu (Congress president 1925), Annie Besant (1917), Kasturba Gandhi , Kamala Nehru , Aruna Asaf Ali (hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank, 1942), Usha Mehta , Sucheta Kripalani , Matangini Hazra , Kanaklata Barua , Captain Lakshmi Sahgal (Rani of Jhansi Regiment, INA).
Women’s organisations and reform

Women’s India Association (1917, Besant); National Council of Women (1925); All India Women’s Conference (1927, Margaret Cousins). Pandita Ramabai , Sharada Sadan; Savitribai Phule ; Begum Rokeya ( Sultana’s Dream , 1905). Bhikaji Cama (Paris, 1907), Madame Cama unfurled a flag at Stuttgart. Rani Gaidinliu (Naga movement), Durgabai Deshmukh and Rani Chennamma earlier.
Dalit politics

Ambedkar : Depressed Classes Conference (1930); Independent Labour Party (1936); Scheduled Castes Federation (1942). Round Table Conferences; Poona Pact (1932). Ayyankali (Kerala, 1893 villuvandi); Mangoo Ram , Ad Dharm movement, Punjab; Jyotirao Phule , Periyar , Iyothee Thass (Tamil). Namasudra movement (Harichand-Guruchand Thakur, Bengal). Gandhi’s Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932) and Congress temple-entry agitation ran alongside.
Tribes and the northeast

Tribal chiefs rose in the 19th century, and later leaders fused with the national cause. Rani Gaidinliu (Heraka movement, Nagaland, 1930s) was jailed by the British; Nehru called her “Rani”. Alluri Sitarama Raju (Rampa, 1922 to 24). Jaipal Singh Munda and the Adivasi Mahasabha (1938) pushed tribal rights. Bhagat Movement among the Oraons (Tana Bhagats, Jatra Bhagat).
Regions and princely states

Punjab : Akali Movement (1920s); Gurdwara Reform Act 1925; Ghadar. Kerala : Vaikom, Guruvayur; Malabar rebellion 1921; Punnapra-Vayalar (1946). Tamil Nadu : Vedaranyam march (Rajaji, 1930). Bengal : Chittagong; Tebhaga. Northwest Frontier : Khudai Khidmatgars (Ghaffar Khan). Princely states : All India States’ Peoples Conference (1927), Praja Mandals.
Labour and left politics

AITUC (1920, Lala Lajpat Rai president), Communist Party (1920s abroad and 1925 Kanpur), Congress Socialist Party (1934; Jayaprakash Narayan, Narendra Dev, Ram Manohar Lohia). Textile strikes (Bombay 1928, Girni Kamgar Union). The Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929) hit the communists.
Was it really a mass movement?

Subaltern Studies says elite-led nationalism missed the people’s own politics. Feminist scholars (Geraldine Forbes, Radha Kumar) note women took part but stayed within domestic and moral roles in public life. Dalit writers question the Congress’s record on caste. A balanced answer shows both participation and exclusions.
Why it matters today

The women’s reservation law, the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam 2023 (106th Amendment), carries this older story. Janjatiya Gaurav Divas (15 November) and rising attention to unsung heroes in the Amrit Mahotsav (2021 to 2023) reflect it. Debates on caste census and social justice are part of the same story.
How to answer

“Women’s participation in the freedom struggle: discuss with examples.” “Role of Ambedkar and Gandhi on the Dalit question.” Prelims tip: Aruna Asaf Ali (1942), Rani Gaidinliu (Heraka), Matangini Hazra (Tamluk), AIWC 1927.
Acts from 1773 to 1935
The constitutional road to 1950
Every Act from 1773 to 1935 made some part of today’s Constitution. The Government of India Act 1935 is the parent of our Constitution. Prelims loves this chain.
Phase 1: Company regulation

Regulating Act 1773 : Governor of Bengal became Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings); Supreme Court at Calcutta; Executive Council of four. Pitt’s India Act 1784 : Board of Control, dual control of Company and Crown. Charter Act 1813 : ended Company’s trade monopoly except tea and China; Rs 1 lakh for education. Charter Act 1833 : Governor-General of India (Bentinck); Law Member added; ended trade completely. Charter Act 1853 : open competition for ICS; legislative members added.
Phase 2: Crown rule

Government of India Act 1858 : Crown took over; Secretary of State and 15-member Council; Viceroy. Indian Councils Act 1861 : Indians nominated to the Viceroy’s council; portfolio system (Canning); legislative devolution to Bombay and Madras. Indian Councils Act 1892 : indirect election and budget discussion.
Morley-Minto Reforms, 1909

Called the Indian Councils Act 1909. More elected members in the Imperial and provincial councils. Indians could ask supplementary questions and move resolutions. Separate electorates for Muslims ; Satyendra Sinha became the first Indian on the Viceroy’s Executive Council. Lord Minto is called the “father of communal electorate”. Morley said he was not aiming at parliamentary government.
Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, 1919

Goal: “progressive realisation of responsible government” (Montagu, 1917). Dyarchy in provinces: transferred subjects (education, health, local government) under Indian ministers; reserved subjects (law and order, finance) under the Governor. Bicameral Centre: Council of State and Legislative Assembly; direct elections but narrow franchise (about 3%). Separate electorates extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians. Public Service Commission and a Statutory Commission after 10 years.
Government of India Act 1935

All India Federation of provinces and princely states (never came into force). Provincial autonomy ; dyarchy shifted to the Centre. Three lists: Federal, Provincial, Concurrent. Federal Court (1937), Reserve Bank (1935), Federal and Provincial Public Service Commissions. Burma separated, Sind and Orissa created. Franchise to about 10% of the population. The Governor’s special powers and the Governor-General’s discretion remained.
Independence Act 1947

The Indian Independence Act 1947 ended British suzerainty over princely states, created two dominions from 15 August 1947, allowed each Constituent Assembly to make laws and to repeal British acts, and ended the office of Secretary of State. Governors-General became constitutional heads. India’s Constituent Assembly became its dominion legislature.
Real reform or divide and rule?

Nationalists saw the Acts as steps taken only under pressure. They used separate electorates and the franchise limits to divide.
