Yet Bipan Chandra and legal historians note the Acts taught provincial administration and gave the Congress the 1937 experience. The 1935 Act is also called a “charter of slavery” by Nehru and “machine with strong brakes and no engine”.
Why it matters today

About 250 provisions of the Constitution come from the 1935 Act: federal scheme, Governor’s office, emergency powers, Public Service Commissions, Federal Court (now Supreme Court) and the three lists. The Reserve Bank still functions under 1934 and 1935 laws. The Governor’s discretion remains a federalism issue today.
How to answer

“The Government of India Act 1935 laid the foundation of the Indian Constitution.” “Trace the constitutional development from 1773 to 1947.” Use a timeline table. Prelims tip: 1773 SC, 1784 Board of Control, 1833 Governor-General of India, 1858 Crown, 1909 separate electorates, 1919 dyarchy, 1935 provincial autonomy.
Partition, Integration of States and Linguistic Reorganisation
Making one nation out of a divided land
In 1947 India was partitioned, hit by mass migration and had 560-plus princely states to bring in. By 1956 it redrew its map on language lines. These are the first tests of the new republic.
Partition and its human cost

Radcliffe’s award (published 17 August 1947) split Punjab and Bengal. Estimates say 10 to 15 million people were displaced and perhaps one million or more died; scholars differ. Refugees from West Punjab, Sindh and East Bengal came to Delhi, Punjab, Bengal. Women were abducted: the Abducted Persons (Recovery and Restoration) Act 1949. Relief and rehabilitation became the first big task; the Ministry of Rehabilitation was set up in 1947. Gandhi went to Noakhali and Calcutta and was killed on 30 January 1948.
Integrating the princely states

Lord Mountbatten and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel , with V. P. Menon as secretary of the States Department, persuaded rulers to sign the Instrument of Accession (defence, external affairs, communications), with the lure of privy purses. All but Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir joined by 15 August 1947. Later: merging into unions (PEPSU, Rajasthan, Madhya Bharat) and “democratisation”. By the 7th Amendment (1956) the Part B states and the princely categories were ended. The privy purse was abolished in the 26th Amendment (1971).
Junagadh, Hyderabad, Kashmir

Junagadh : Muslim ruler, mostly Hindu population, acceded to Pakistan; India held a plebiscite (Feb 1948) and it joined India. Hyderabad : the Nizam wanted independence. Operation Polo (police action, 13 to 18 September 1948) ended his rule. Kashmir : Maharaja Hari Singh acceded on 26 October 1947 after tribal raiders backed by Pakistan; India took the matter to the UN (1 January 1948); ceasefire 1 January 1949 (effective); Article 370 gave a special position (abrogated on 5 August 2019).
Other integration

Goa, Daman and Diu: Liberated by Operation Vijay (December 1961). Pondicherry: de facto transfer in 1954, de jure 1962. Sikkim: became a state in 1975 (36th Amendment). Dadra and Nagar Haveli (1954 taken over by local people). The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, with the States Reorganisation still pending.
Linguistic reorganisation

The Dar Commission (1948) was against it; the JVP Committee (Jawaharlal, Vallabhbhai, Pattabhi, 1948) said “not now”. After Potti Sriramulu died on fast (December 1952), Andhra State was formed (1953). The States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali, K. M. Panikkar, H. N. Kunzru, 1953 to 55) recommended 16 states and 3 centrally administered territories. The States Reorganisation Act 1956 : 14 states and 6 UTs. Later: Bombay split into Maharashtra and Gujarat (1960), Punjab and Haryana (1966), Nagaland (1963), Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura (1972), Mizoram and Arunachal (1987), and in 2000, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand; Telangana (2014).
Constitutional basis

Articles 2 to 4: Parliament can admit or establish new states, alter areas, boundaries or names by a simple majority (not a constitutional amendment under Article 368). The President refers the Bill to the State Legislature for its views, which are not binding (Babulal Parante, 1960). Supreme Court: Berubari Union case (1960). The 2019 Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act used Article 3 to create UTs of J&K and Ladakh.
Was language the right basis?

Fears of fragmentation proved wrong: Nehru’s fear gave way to a federal strength. Ramachandra Guha and Granville Austin note that linguistic states made democracy work by giving regions a voice. Critics point to new demands: sub-regional (Telangana, Vidarbha), river water and border disputes (Belgaum, Cauvery). The three-language formula and language agitations (Anti-Hindi in Tamil Nadu 1965) show the limits.
Why it matters today

Hyderabad Liberation Day (17 September), National Unity Day (31 October, Patel’s birth anniversary; the Statue of Unity at Kevadia, 2018) show how integration is remembered. Border disputes, J&K’s status and demands for statehood and Sixth Schedule rights (Ladakh) are live. The Partition Horrors Remembrance Day (14 August) was declared in 2021.
How to answer

“The integration of princely states was an act of statecraft. Discuss.” “Linguistic reorganisation strengthened Indian unity. Comment.” Prelims tip: Operation Polo 1948; Goa 1961; SRC 1953 to 55; Act 1956; Gujarat and Maharashtra 1960; Haryana 1966; Telangana 2014; Articles 2 to 4.
Nehru Era: Planning, Foreign Policy and Institutions
The nation-building decade
From 1947 to 1964 India set its institutions, economy and foreign stance. Many debates about the state and the market begin here.
Institutions

A Constitution (1950), universal adult franchise, first general elections 1951 to 52 (about 173 million voters; Election Commission under Sukumar Sen), Parliament, an independent judiciary, civilian control of the army, the Planning Commission (March 1950), National Development Council (1952). The Hindu Code Bills (1955 to 56) reformed personal law. The IITs (Kharagpur, 1951), AIIMS (1956), CSIR, ISRO’s ancestors (Atomic Energy Commission, 1948, Homi Bhabha).
Planning and the economy

First Plan (1951 to 56): Harrod-Domar model, agriculture, irrigation (Bhakra, Hirakud). Second Plan (1956 to 61): P. C. Mahalanobis; heavy industry; steel plants (Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur). Industrial Policy Resolution 1956: mixed economy with a public sector. Third Plan (1961 to 66): self-reliance; war in 1962 and 1965 disrupted. Land reforms: zamindari abolition, tenancy laws, ceilings; Bhoodan (Vinoba Bhave, 1951). Community Development (1952), Panchayati Raj (Balwant Rai Mehta Committee 1957; Rajasthan 1959).
Foreign policy: non-alignment

Nehru’s idea of Non-Alignment : independence from both blocs. Panchsheel with China (1954); Bandung (1955); Suez (1956, India opposed the attack); Hungary (1956, abstained); NAM (1961, Belgrade); Korea (mediation); Congo (peacekeeping). Principles: anti-colonialism, anti-racism (South Africa), disarmament. Ties with the USSR grew; India stayed in the Commonwealth.
The 1962 war

Border problems: Aksai Chin, McMahon Line, Tibet’s revolt (1959) and the Dalai Lama’s asylum. China attacked on 20 October 1962 and declared a ceasefire on 21 November. India lost Aksai Chin territory and morale; Defence Minister Krishna Menon resigned. The war led to the Henderson Brooks inquiry (not fully public), higher defence spending and a rethink of idealism.
Kashmir and other issues

1947 to 48 war; UN resolution (August 1948 and January 1949); Indus Waters Treaty 1960 (World Bank); Nehru-Liaquat Pact 1950; Naga insurgency; Goa 1961; border settlement with Burma. Language and reorganisation of states. The Congress dominance: the Congress system (Rajni Kothari).
Was the Nehruvian model a success?

Admirers (Bipan Chandra, Mridula Mukherjee) point to a stable democracy, heavy industry and scientific institutions. Critics say the focus on heavy industry slowed agriculture and education, caused licence-permit raj and left a “Hindu rate of growth” (Raj Krishna). Others (Tirthankar Roy) argue the 1950s growth was decent. Foreign policy: idealism or realism?
Why it matters today

The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015. Non-alignment evolved into “strategic autonomy” and multi-alignment. Institutions such as the Election Commission, IITs and public sector remain. Panchsheel’s 70th anniversary (2024) was marked amid India-China talks.
How to answer

“Evaluate Nehru’s contribution to nation building.” “Merits and demerits of the Mahalanobis model.” “Why did India lose the 1962 war?” Prelims tip: Planning Commission 1950; First Plan 1951; Second Plan 1956; IPR 1956; Panchsheel 1954; Balwant Rai 1957; 1962 war; Indus Treaty 1960.
1965–1991: Wars, Emergency and Coalitions
From one-party dominance to a messy democracy
The 1960s to 80s saw wars, economic crisis, Indira Gandhi’s rise, the Emergency and the first non-Congress governments. UPSC loves cause-and-effect here.
After Nehru

Nehru died on 27 May 1964. Lal Bahadur Shastri became PM; the Green Revolution and the White Revolution (Verghese Kurien’s Operation Flood, 1970) began. The 1965 war with Pakistan (Operation Gibraltar; Rann of Kutch; ceasefire; Tashkent Declaration , 10 January 1966; Shastri died there). The 1966 devaluation of the rupee and drought hurt.
Indira Gandhi and the Congress split

Indira Gandhi became PM in January 1966 (“goongi gudiya”). 1967 elections: Congress lost seats and eight states; coalitions (SVD governments) appeared. 1969: Congress split (Syndicate vs Indira); bank nationalisation (14 banks), the privy purse abolition attempt; “Garibi Hatao” (1971 election, big win). 1971: Bangladesh war ; the Shimla Agreement (1972). 1974: first nuclear test at Pokhran (“Smiling Buddha”).
The JP movement and the Emergency

Navnirman (Gujarat) and the Bihar movement (1974); Jayaprakash Narayan ’s call for “total revolution”. Allahabad High Court (12 June 1975, Justice Sinha) found Indira guilty of electoral malpractice ( Raj Narain case). Emergency proclaimed 25 June 1975 under Article 352 (internal disturbance): opponents jailed, press censored, MISA, forced sterilisation (Sanjay Gandhi), slum demolitions. The 42nd Amendment (1976) extended the Lok Sabha term to six years and added “socialist”, “secular”, Fundamental Duties.
Janata, return and later years

Emergency lifted 21 March 1977. In the 1977 election the Janata Party won; Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress PM. The Shah Commission. The 44th Amendment (1978) made “internal disturbance” into “armed rebellion” and restored rights. Janata collapsed; Charan Singh briefly; Indira returned in January 1980. Punjab militancy; Operation Blue Star (June 1984); assassination of Indira Gandhi (31 October 1984) and anti-Sikh riots. Rajiv Gandhi won 1984 with 400-plus seats.
Rajiv Gandhi to 1991

Rajiv’s early reforms: anti-defection law (52nd Amendment, 1985), Assam and Punjab accords, telecom and computers. Controversies: the Shah Bano case and the Muslim Women Act (1986), Ayodhya locks opened, Bofors, IPKF in Sri Lanka (1987 to 90). 1989: V. P. Singh ’s National Front; Mandal Commission recommendations (7 August 1990; 27% OBC reservation). Rath Yatra (L. K. Advani, 1990). Chandra Shekhar (1990 to 91) and the foreign exchange crisis. Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated on 21 May 1991. Narasimha Rao and liberalisation followed.
Economy and society

Green Revolution (M. S. Swaminathan, Norman Borlaug; HYV wheat in Punjab, Haryana, west UP); food self-sufficiency by the late 1970s. Planning slowed; the oil shocks (1973, 1979) and balance of payments strains. Rise of regional parties (DMK, Akali Dal, TDP in 1982, AGP 1985) and social movements (Chipko, Dalit Panthers 1972, farmers).
Emergency: aberration or logic of centralisation?

Supporters said it restored order; critics call it the darkest chapter. Scholars (Rudolph and Rudolph, Granville Austin) see a crisis of institutions and the personalisation of power. The Basic Structure doctrine ( Kesavananda Bharati , 1973) and the ADM Jabalpur case (1976, widely seen as wrong; overruled in effect by Puttaswamy , 2017) are central. Some say the 1989 shift began coalition politics.
Why it matters today

25 June is observed as “Samvidhan Hatya Diwas” (since 2024). The Basic Structure doctrine, press freedom and anti-defection law (10th Schedule) come from this era. Coalition governments from 1989 to 2014 shaped federalism and policy, before the BJP’s 2014 majority. The Mandal debate continues in caste census talks.
How to answer

“The Emergency: causes, impact and lessons.” “Why did coalition governments emerge in India?” “Green Revolution: benefits and costs.” Prelims tip: Tashkent 1966; split 1969; Shimla 1972; Pokhran 1974; Emergency 1975 to 77; Mandal 1990; 52nd Amendment 1985; 42nd Amendment 1976.
Industrial Revolution
The break that made the modern world
From about 1760 Britain moved from hand work to machines. This changed cities, classes, empires and India’s economy. UPSC asks for causes, effects and the link to colonialism.
Why Britain first

Agricultural revolution and enclosures freed labour and raised food output. Capital from trade, slavery and colonies; Bank of England and credit. Coal and iron near each other; rivers and canals. Colonial markets and raw cotton. Political stability after 1688; patents; a culture of science (Royal Society). Population growth.
Inventions

Textiles : John Kay’s flying shuttle (1733), Hargreaves’s spinning jenny (1764), Arkwright’s water frame (1769), Crompton’s mule (1779), Cartwright’s power loom (1785), Whitney’s cotton gin (1793, USA). Steam : Newcomen (1712), James Watt (separate condenser, 1769). Iron : Abraham Darby coke smelting (1709); Henry Cort’s puddling (1784). Transport : Stephenson’s locomotive; Stockton and Darlington line (1825); Liverpool-Manchester (1830).
Phases

First revolution (c. 1760 to 1830): textiles, steam, coal, iron. Second (c. 1870 to 1914): steel (Bessemer, 1856), electricity, chemicals, oil, the internal combustion engine, mass production. Germany and the USA led the second. Third and fourth: electronics and digital technology, in debate.
Social effects

Factory system; urbanisation (Manchester, Birmingham); new classes: industrial bourgeoisie and working class. Child and women labour, long hours, slums, disease. Reform: Factory Acts (1833, 1847 ten-hour day), Poor Law, trade unions, Chartism (1838), Combination Acts repealed 1824. Ideas: Adam Smith ( Wealth of Nations , 1776), Malthus, Ricardo; Marx and Engels’s Communist Manifesto (1848); Robert Owen’s model village.
Effect on the colonies

India’s textile exports declined as Lancashire cloth came in; India became a market for British goods and a source of raw cotton, jute and indigo. Egypt and America supplied cotton. Africa supplied slaves and later raw materials. The need for markets and raw materials pushed the “new imperialism” after 1870. Rail and telegraph spread the system.
Revolution or evolution?

Arnold Toynbee (1884) coined the term. Later economic historians (Crafts, Harley) say growth was slow and gradual. E. P. Thompson ( The Making of the English Working Class , 1963) stressed the human cost. Eric Williams ( Capitalism and Slavery , 1944) linked slave profits to industrial capital; this is still debated. Kenneth Pomeranz ( The Great Divergence , 2000) points to coal and colonies.
Why it matters today

India’s early industry: the first cotton mill (Bombay, 1854, Cowasji Davar), jute mills (Calcutta), TISCO (Jamshedpur, 1907). Debates on the fourth industrial revolution, AI and jobs echo the old fear of machines. The question of climate change and historic emissions links back to coal-led industrialisation.
How to answer

“Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in England?” “Industrial Revolution and its impact on the colonies.” Prelims tip: Watt (steam), Hargreaves (jenny), Arkwright (water frame), Crompton (mule), Cartwright (power loom), Stephenson (rail 1825).
American and French Revolutions
Rights, republics and nations
These two revolutions gave the world the ideas of popular sovereignty, rights and the nation. Many Indian constitutional ideas trace to them.
American Revolution: causes

After the Seven Years’ War (1756 to 63), Britain taxed the 13 colonies: Sugar Act (1764), Stamp Act (1765), Townshend duties (1767), Tea Act (1773). Colonists said “no taxation without representation”. Boston Massacre (1770), Boston Tea Party (1773) . The Intolerable (Coercive) Acts (1774). The First Continental Congress (1774).
War and Declaration

Fighting began at Lexington and Concord (1775). The Declaration of Independence (4 July 1776, drafted by Thomas Jefferson) cited Locke’s ideas of life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Victory at Saratoga (1777) brought French aid. Yorktown (1781). Treaty of Paris, 1783. George Washington led the army. Thomas Paine’s Common Sense (1776) swayed opinion.
The US Constitution

Philadelphia Convention (1787). Federalism, separation of powers, checks and balances, written constitution, a Bill of Rights (first ten amendments, 1791). Judicial review followed in Marbury v. Madison (1803). Features that influenced India: fundamental rights, judicial review, preamble, federal idea, impeachment, Vice-President as Rajya Sabha-type chair (Chairman).
French Revolution: causes

Old Regime: three estates; clergy and nobles exempt from most taxes; Third Estate paid. Financial crisis: wars and court costs; failed reforms (Turgot, Necker, Calonne). Enlightenment ideas: Montesquieu, Voltaire, Rousseau ( Social Contract , 1762). Bad harvests and bread prices (1788 to 89).
Course of the Revolution

1789: Estates-General; Tennis Court Oath; Fall of the Bastille, 14 July ; Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen (August). 1791: Constitutional monarchy. 1792: Republic; the king, Louis XVI, executed in January 1793. Reign of Terror (1793 to 94, Robespierre, Committee of Public Safety). 1795: Directory. 1799: Napoleon’s coup.
Napoleon and the legacy

Napoleon Bonaparte became First Consul (1799), Emperor (1804). The Napoleonic Code (1804) spread legal equality, property rights and merit. He was defeated at Waterloo (1815). Congress of Vienna (1815, Metternich) restored monarchy. Legacy: liberty, equality, fraternity; the nation-state; secularism; metric system; end of feudal dues; slogan inspired the 1848 revolutions and, through Rammohun Roy, Indian liberals.
Origins and meaning

Marxist historians (Georges Lefebvre) saw a bourgeois revolution. Revisionists (Alfred Cobban, François Furet) say the bourgeoisie was not a unified class and stressed politics and ideas. R. R. Palmer proposed an “Atlantic revolution” linking America and France. Slavery and the Haitian Revolution (1791 to 1804) show limits of the universal claim.
Why it matters today

The Preamble’s “liberty, equality, fraternity”, Fundamental Rights and judicial review reflect these revolutions. Tipu Sultan is said to have planted a liberty tree at Seringapatam; Indian press celebrated Bastille Day. Ambedkar cited the French trio but traced fraternity to Buddha.
How to answer

“Compare American and French Revolutions.” “Influence of the French Revolution on India or the world.” Prelims tip: Declaration of Independence 1776; Constitution 1787; Bastille 1789; Rights of Man 1789; Terror 1793 to 94; Napoleon’s Code 1804.
Nationalism: Unification of Italy and Germany
Making nation-states
The nationalism that Europe’s revolutions spread made new states in 1861 and 1871. UPSC asks for the role of leaders and methods, and for comparisons.
After Vienna

The Congress of Vienna (1815) split Italy into states under Austria and the Bourbons; Germany became a 39-state German Confederation led by Austria. Liberal and national movements rose: revolutions of 1830 and 1848 (the “spring of nations”). They mostly failed, but the idea of a nation had taken root.
Italy: the thinkers

Giuseppe Mazzini founded the Carbonari-era Young Italy (1831) and wanted a republic. Cavour , prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia under King Victor Emmanuel II, wanted a monarchy through diplomacy. Garibaldi led the Red Shirts. Austria was the main enemy. The Risorgimento (resurgence) was both ideas and war.
Italy: the steps

1859: Cavour allied with Napoleon III against Austria (Plombières, 1858); Lombardy gained. 1860: Garibaldi’s thousand Red Shirts took Sicily and Naples. 1861: Kingdom of Italy proclaimed; Victor Emmanuel II king. 1866: Venetia (after the Austro-Prussian war). 1870: Rome taken when French troops withdrew.
Germany: the route

Zollverein (1834): a customs union led by Prussia. Bismarck (minister-president from 1862): “blood and iron”, Realpolitik . Wars: against Denmark (1864; Schleswig-Holstein), Austria (1866, Sadowa/Königgrätz; the North German Confederation), France (1870 to 71, Sedan). On 18 January 1871 William I was proclaimed German emperor at Versailles.
The 1871 empire

A federal empire with a strong Prussian king, a Reichstag elected by universal male suffrage and a chancellor who answered to the emperor. Bismarck’s later policy: Kulturkampf against Catholics, anti-socialist laws and welfare, alliance system (Three Emperors’ League, Triple Alliance 1882), Berlin Congress (1878) and conference (1884 to 85). He was dismissed by William II in 1890.
Idea or power?

Italy was made by diplomacy and foreign help more than people’s rising; Germany by Prussian power. A. J. P. Taylor ( The Struggle for Mastery in Europe ) saw Bismarck as an opportunist. Historians such as Hans-Ulrich Wehler see “top-down” unification. Liberals thought unity meant freedom; instead it meant strong states.
Why it matters today

Indian leaders in the 1900s drew on Mazzini; Savarkar translated Mazzini’s writings; Tilak and the Extremists admired Garibaldi. India’s integration of princely states in 1947 (Patel as the “Bismarck of India”) is often compared. Debates on nationalism, federalism and diversity in a union echo the German model.
How to answer

“Compare the unification of Italy and Germany.” Table: leaders, methods, states, outcome. “Role of Bismarck.” Prelims tip: Zollverein 1834; Italy 1861; Rome 1870; Sedan 1870; German Empire proclaimed 1871 at Versailles.
Colonialism and Imperialism in Asia and Africa
Why Europe ruled the world
From about 1870 Europe took Africa and much of Asia. The questions: why, how, and how did people respond? India sits at the centre of this story.
Old and new imperialism

Old: trade posts and mercantile empires (1500 to 1800). New (c. 1870 to 1914): direct rule, led by industrial powers needing raw materials, markets, investment and prestige. Hobson ( Imperialism , 1902) and Lenin ( Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism , 1916) offered economic explanations; Joseph Schumpeter and others added politics. Social Darwinism and the “white man’s burden” (Kipling, 1899) gave moral cover.
Tools of empire

Quinine, steamships, the Maxim gun, telegraph and railways. The Suez Canal (1869) and Berlin Conference (1884 to 85) set rules for the “Scramble for Africa”. The Congo Free State (Leopold II) became a symbol of cruelty. By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia were free in Africa. British, French, German, Belgian, Italian and Portuguese empires divided the continent.
Asia

India : British Raj after 1858. China : Opium Wars (1839 to 42; 1856 to 60), Treaty of Nanking (1842; Hong Kong ceded), treaty ports, Taiping Rebellion (1850 to 64), Boxer Rebellion (1899 to 1901), Open Door policy (US, 1899), 1911 revolution (Sun Yat-sen). Japan : Perry (1853), Meiji Restoration (1868), defeat of China (1894 to 95) and Russia (1904 to 05). Southeast Asia : Dutch East Indies, French Indochina, British Burma and Malaya, Siam as a buffer.
Resistance

Early resistance was local and often by old elites (Abyssinia, Zulu, Ashanti, Mahdi in Sudan, Samori in West Africa, Maji Maji in German East Africa). Later movements were national: Indian National Congress (1885), Young Turks, Sun Yat-sen’s Tongmenghui, the Vietnamese nationalists. The Japanese victory in 1905 inspired many Asian leaders including Indians.
Colonial economies

Cash crops (cotton, rubber, coffee, cocoa), mining (diamonds, gold in South Africa; copper in the Congo), indentured labour moved millions, including Indians to Mauritius, Fiji, the Caribbean, South Africa and Malaya. Borders drawn in Berlin cut across peoples, a source of later conflict. Education and bureaucracy created a small westernised elite who later led independence.
Did colonial rule modernise?

Defenders (Niall Ferguson) argue empire spread law, trade and institutions. Critics (Walter Rodney, How Europe Underdeveloped Africa , 1972; Edward Said, Orientalism , 1978) argue it caused underdevelopment and a cultural hold. Mike Davis ( Late Victorian Holocausts , 2001) ties famines to colonial policy. The debate on reparations continues.
Why it matters today

Africa and India share a history of colonialism; Gandhi in South Africa, the Non-Aligned Movement and Bandung (1955) grew from it. India’s Africa policy, the African Union’s admission to the G20 (2023, under India’s presidency) and debates on restitution of artefacts and apologies (Jallianwala Bagh) make this live.
How to answer

“The Scramble for Africa: causes and effects.” “Economic and political imperialism: Hobson and Lenin.” “Impact of colonialism on Asia and Africa.” Prelims tip: Berlin Conference 1884 to 85; Suez 1869; Treaty of Nanking 1842; Meiji 1868; Open Door 1899.
First World War and the Russian Revolution
Two events that remade the century
The Great War ended four empires. The Russian Revolution created the first communist state. India’s war role and Wilson’s ideas shaped Indian politics.
Causes of the war

The classic list is MAIN : Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism. The two blocs: Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia). Crises: Morocco (1905, 1911), the Balkan Wars (1912 to 13), naval race. Fritz Fischer (1961) stressed German war aims; others stress a failure of diplomacy.
Outbreak and course

The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo (28 June 1914) by Gavrilo Princip led to Austria’s ultimatum to Serbia and a chain of declarations. Germany’s Schlieffen Plan led to the invasion of Belgium; Britain entered. Western Front trench warfare (Marne 1914, Verdun and Somme 1916). Eastern Front: Russia’s defeats (Tannenberg). Italy joined the Entente in 1915; the Ottomans joined Germany. The USA entered on 6 April 1917 after unrestricted submarine war and the Zimmermann telegram. Armistice: 11 November 1918.
Peace settlement

Paris Peace Conference (1919): Wilson, Clemenceau, Lloyd George. Wilson’s Fourteen Points (self-determination, League of Nations). Treaty of Versailles (28 June 1919): war guilt clause (Article 231), reparations (fixed at 132 billion gold marks in 1921), loss of territory, army cap of 100,000. Other treaties: Saint-Germain (Austria), Trianon (Hungary), Neuilly (Bulgaria), Sèvres (Turkey), later Lausanne (1923). League of Nations began 1920; the USA never joined. Keynes called the peace “Carthaginian”.
Russia before 1917

Tsar Nicholas II ruled an autocracy with poor peasants and a small, growing working class. Defeat in Japan (1905) led to the 1905 revolution and the Duma. Rasputin’s influence and war losses broke trust. Marxist parties: Mensheviks and Bolsheviks (split 1903, Lenin).

February (March) Revolution : strikes in Petrograd; Tsar abdicated; Provisional Government (Kerensky). Lenin’s April Theses : “Peace, Land and Bread”, “all power to the Soviets”. October (November) Revolution : Bolsheviks (Trotsky’s Military Revolutionary Committee) seized the Winter Palace, 25 October (Old Style). Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918): Russia left the war, losing large areas.
Civil war and the new state

The Civil War (1918 to 1921): Reds versus Whites and foreign forces; Red Terror; War Communism. New Economic Policy (NEP, 1921) allowed small private trade. USSR founded in December 1922. After Lenin’s death (1924), Stalin won against Trotsky; Five-Year Plans (from 1928), collectivisation, the purges. Comintern (1919) spread communism.
Revolution or coup?

Soviet writers saw a working-class revolution. Western historians such as Richard Pipes called it a coup. Revisionists (Sheila Fitzpatrick) stress the mass support of workers and soldiers. E. H. Carr ( The Bolshevik Revolution ) treated it as a historic necessity. Debate on Versailles: too harsh (Keynes) or not harsh enough (Foch)?
Why it matters today

About 1.3 million Indians served; around 74,000 died; the Indian Army fought in France, Mesopotamia and East Africa; the India Gate (1931) commemorates them. The war brought the Home Rule League, the Lucknow Pact (1916), Montagu Declaration and Rowlatt Act. The Russian Revolution inspired Indian communists (M. N. Roy at Comintern 1920, CPI 1920 to 25) and Nehru’s socialism; the NEP and Five-Year Plans influenced Indian planning.
How to answer

“Causes of the First World War: was Germany solely responsible?” “Why did the Russian Revolution occur in 1917?” “Impact of the war on India.” Prelims tip: Sarajevo 1914; US entry 1917; Brest-Litovsk 1918; Versailles 1919; League 1920; NEP 1921; USSR 1922.
Interwar Years, Fascism and the Second World War
The collapse of peace
From the Great Depression to Hiroshima, the 1930s and 1940s made the world we have now: the UN, the Cold War, decolonisation and the nuclear age.
The Depression and its effects

The Wall Street Crash (October 1929) began the Great Depression . Banks failed; trade shrank; unemployment soared. The USA’s answer was Roosevelt’s New Deal (1933). Britain left the gold standard. Many states turned to extremes. Economists: Keynes ( General Theory , 1936).
Fascism and Nazism

Italy : Mussolini; March on Rome 1922; one-party state, corporatism. Germany : Hitler; Beer Hall Putsch 1923; Mein Kampf ; Chancellor January 1933; Reichstag fire; Enabling Act (March 1933); Nuremberg Laws (1935); Kristallnacht (1938). Features: extreme nationalism, leader cult, anti-communism, racism, militarism. Japan: militarism after 1931 (Manchuria). Spain: Franco (1936 to 39).
Road to war

1931 Japan seizes Manchuria; League fails. 1935 Italy invades Ethiopia; Germany re-arms. 1936 Rhineland; Rome-Berlin Axis; Anti-Comintern Pact. 1938 Anschluss; Munich Agreement (Chamberlain’s appeasement). 1939 Hitler takes Czechoslovakia; Nazi-Soviet Pact (August); invasion of Poland (1 September).
The war

1939 to 41: Blitzkrieg; fall of France (June 1940); Battle of Britain; invasion of the USSR (June 1941; Operation Barbarossa); Pearl Harbor (7 December 1941) brought the USA in. Turning points: Stalingrad (1942 to 43), Midway (1942), El Alamein. D-Day (6 June 1944). Germany surrendered 8 May 1945. The USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima (6 August) and Nagasaki (9 August 1945). Japan surrendered on 15 August (signed 2 September). The Holocaust killed six million Jews.
Peace conferences

Atlantic Charter (1941), Tehran (1943), Yalta (February 1945), Potsdam (July to August 1945). Nuremberg and Tokyo trials. United Nations formed 24 October 1945 (San Francisco conference); Security Council with five veto-holding permanent members. Bretton Woods (1944): IMF and World Bank. Germany divided into four zones.
Causes and blame

A. J. P. Taylor ( Origins of the Second World War , 1961) saw Hitler as an opportunist and appeasement as understandable; others (Trevor-Roper) saw a clear plan in Mein Kampf. Versailles, the Depression, the failure of the League and appeasement all matter. E. H. Carr’s Twenty Years’ Crisis (1939) calls utopianism a cause.
Why it matters today

India was dragged into the war without consultation (1939), leading to Congress resignation and Quit India. Over 2.5 million Indians served, the largest volunteer army, and the Bengal famine (1943) killed up to three million. India’s Subhas Bose allied with the Axis; INA trials followed. India was a founding UN member (1945) and Radhabinod Pal sat at the Tokyo trial as a dissenting judge. India’s UN Security Council claim comes from this settlement.
How to answer

“Analyse the causes of the Second World War.” “Fascism and Nazism: similarities and differences.” “Effects of the war on India’s freedom struggle.” Prelims tip: Munich 1938; Nazi-Soviet pact Aug 1939; Pearl Harbor 7 Dec 1941; D-Day 1944; UN 1945; Hiroshima 6 Aug 1945.
Decolonisation and the Cold War
The two big stories of the late 20th century
Between 1945 and 1991 the colonies became states and the world split into two blocs. India was in the middle: it freed first, then led non-alignment.
Why empires ended

War exhaustion of Britain, France and the Netherlands; rise of the USA and USSR (both anti-colonial in speech); nationalist movements; the UN Charter’s self-determination; and the example of India (1947). Methods: negotiation (India, Ghana 1957), war (Algeria 1954 to 62, Vietnam), settler resistance (Kenya, Mau Mau), settler states (Rhodesia, South Africa). Portugal clung on until 1974 (Carnation Revolution).
Waves of decolonisation

1945 to 1950s : India, Pakistan, Burma, Ceylon (1947 to 48), Indonesia (1949), Vietnam (Dien Bien Phu 1954). 1960 , the “Year of Africa”: 17 states. 1960s to 70s : Algeria 1962, Kenya 1963, Angola and Mozambique 1975, Zimbabwe 1980, Namibia 1990. South Africa’s end of apartheid (1994, Mandela). Bandung Conference (1955), Non-Aligned Movement (Belgrade, 1961; Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Nkrumah, Sukarno).
Origins of the Cold War

Ideological gap between capitalism and communism; the Soviet hold on Eastern Europe; mutual fear. Churchill’s “iron curtain” speech (1946). Truman Doctrine (1947, aid to Greece and Turkey); Marshall Plan (1948, about $13 billion); Cominform; Berlin Blockade (1948 to 49) and the airlift. NATO (1949); Warsaw Pact (1955). Containment (George Kennan’s Long Telegram, 1946).
Crises and phases

1949: Soviet bomb; Chinese revolution. 1950 to 53: Korean War . 1956: Hungary, Suez. 1961: Berlin Wall. 1962: Cuban Missile Crisis ; hotline in 1963; Partial Test Ban Treaty 1963. 1965 to 75: Vietnam war. Détente (1970s): SALT I (1972), Helsinki Accords (1975). 1979: Soviet invasion of Afghanistan; “new Cold War”.
End of the Cold War

Gorbachev (from 1985): glasnost and perestroika ; INF Treaty (1987); fall of the Berlin Wall (9 November 1989); German unification (October 1990); Warsaw Pact ended (1991); failed coup (August 1991); the USSR dissolved on 26 December 1991. Reasons: economic stagnation, arms race costs, Afghanistan, nationalism, and Reagan’s pressure.
Who started it?

Orthodox (traditionalist) writers blamed Stalin; revisionists such as William Appleman Williams and Gabriel Kolko blamed US economic expansion; post-revisionists such as John Lewis Gaddis ( We Now Know , 1997) found fault on both sides. Francis Fukuyama’s “end of history” (1989) was challenged by Huntington’s Clash of Civilizations (1993).
Why it matters today

India’s non-alignment was a form of strategic autonomy; its 1971 treaty with the USSR; its role in Korea (Custodian Force, Chair of the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission, K. P. S. Thimayya). Today’s “multi-alignment” and the new great-power rivalry between the US and China are debated as a possible “new Cold War”.
How to answer

“Discuss the role of NAM in the Cold War.” “Decolonisation of Africa: patterns and problems.” “Why did the Cold War end?” Prelims tip: Truman 1947; Marshall 1948; NATO 1949; Warsaw 1955; Cuba 1962; Berlin Wall 1961 and 1989; USSR dissolved Dec 1991.
Political Philosophies: Capitalism, Socialism, Communism
Ideas behind the blocs
UPSC asks you to define each ideology, name its thinkers and compare how they work. Many Indian economic debates sit between these poles.
Capitalism

Private ownership, markets, profit and competition. Adam Smith ( The Wealth of Nations , 1776): the “invisible hand”. Laissez-faire (Ricardo, Mill). After the Depression, Keynes argued for state action to keep up demand. Later Hayek and Milton Friedman returned to free markets (neoliberalism; Thatcher and Reagan in the 1980s). Forms: welfare capitalism (Scandinavia), state capitalism (China).
Socialism

Social ownership or control of the means of production and equality. Early or utopian socialists: Saint-Simon, Fourier, Robert Owen. Fabians (UK, 1884): gradual change. Social democracy (Bernstein, revisionism). Welfare states: Beveridge Report (1942), UK’s NHS (1948). Democratic socialism seeks socialism by the ballot.
Marx and Engels

Communist Manifesto (1848): history as class struggle. Das Kapital (vol. 1, 1867): surplus value and exploitation. Historical (dialectical) materialism: base and superstructure. Stages: feudalism, capitalism, socialism, then communism. The proletariat’s revolution leads to a “dictatorship of the proletariat”. Later: Lenin (vanguard party, imperialism), Stalin, Mao (peasant revolution, 1949), Gramsci (hegemony).
Communism in practice

USSR (1917 to 91): planned economy, collectivisation, one-party rule. China: Mao’s Great Leap Forward (1958 to 62), Cultural Revolution (1966 to 76); Deng’s reforms from 1978 (“socialism with Chinese characteristics”). Cuba, Vietnam, North Korea. Eastern Europe’s regimes fell in 1989. Gains: literacy, heavy industry; costs: lack of freedom and famines.
Mixed economy and the third way

Most states mix market and state. India: Nehru’s mixed economy; Industrial Policy Resolution 1956. Western Europe: social market economy. Anthony Giddens’s Third Way (1998) shaped Blair. China uses markets under party control. After the 2008 crisis the role of the state returned to debate.
Which system works?

Defenders of capitalism cite growth and innovation; critics cite inequality (Thomas Piketty, Capital in the Twenty-First Century , 2013) and climate costs. Socialists cite fairness; critics cite inefficiency and lack of freedom (Hayek, The Road to Serfdom , 1944). Fukuyama thought liberal democracy had won; today’s populism and state capitalism challenge that.
Why it matters today

The word “socialist” was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976). Nehru wanted a socialistic pattern (Avadi Congress, 1955); Gandhi’s trusteeship and Ambedkar’s state socialism were alternatives. 1991 liberalisation moved India towards markets, while welfare schemes (MGNREGA 2005; NFSA 2013) show the mixed path.
How to answer

“Compare capitalism and socialism with examples.” “Marx’s theory of historical materialism: assess.” “India’s economic path: socialist, capitalist or mixed?” Prelims tip: Smith 1776; Manifesto 1848; Capital 1867; Fabian 1884; Keynes 1936; Hayek 1944; Preamble “socialist” 1976.
